papers.title: Robust Aggregation of Quantile Statistics: from Median to Interval
papers.abstract: Quantile-based summaries, such as prediction intervals and medians, are commonly used in economic forecasting, climate science, and public health. For highly skewed samples, experimental evidence suggests that estimates of the mean can be biased toward the median, whereas estimates of the median are relatively accurate. This motivates aggregating explicitly elicited quantiles rather than reported means. We study robust aggregation of quantile reports for bounded outcomes under squared loss, minimizing worst-case regret relative to an omniscient Bayesian aggregator who knows the information structure and observes all private signals. Without restrictions on the information structure, no rule improves on the constant forecast at the range midpoint in worst-case regret. We therefore consider weak substitutes, a diminishing-returns condition on the value of information, and characterize optimal aggregation rules under this condition. For central prediction intervals with common nominal coverage $α$, the optimal rule, which we call regularized simple average for prediction intervals, shrinks the average reported interval midpoint toward the range midpoint, with a weight determined by $α$ and the number $n$ of experts. This optimal rule strictly improves on the constant baseline in worst-case regret when $α<1/\sqrt{n}$; at or above this threshold, the constant rule is optimal. The optimal worst-case regret is minimized at a unique interior coverage level, revealing a nonmonotonic relationship between coverage and aggregation performance. For median reports, regularized simple average for medians similarly shrinks the average reported median toward the range midpoint, assigning weight $1/n$ to the reported average and strictly improving on the constant baseline in worst-case regret for every finite $n\ge2$.

papers.title: An exact unstable mode of self-similar Yang--Mills solutionsin 5+1 dimensions
papers.abstract: Self-similar solutions play an important role in the formation of singularities in the Yang--Mills equations. In five space dimensions, these equations admit infinitely many self-similar solutions with an increasing number of unstable modes. It was observed numerically that all excited profiles share the least unstable eigenvalue $λ=5$. We explain this remarkable spectral property by an elementary construction of the corresponding eigenfunction in terms of the profile.

papers.title: On Douglas' conjecture for $m$-Kronecker quivers
papers.abstract: We prove Douglas' conjecture for $m$-Kronecker quivers for each $m \geq 3$ on the normalized logarithms of Euler characteristics of moduli spaces. Also, we state a log-concavity conjecture on Euler characteristics near slope one for the 3-Kronecker quiver.

papers.title: Geometric Obstructions and Sharp Genus Dependence in LCD Scalings
papers.abstract: We study the least pole order of a rational function whose nonzero evaluations scale a prescribed code to a Euclidean LCD code. A residue-one differential yields an obstruction for odd-dimensional one-point AG codes in characteristic two: for $C=C_L(D,aQ)$ with $0\le a<n$ and odd dimension, the threshold is at least $n+2g-a-1$. The obstruction uses alternating Gram matrices and does not require the scaled code to be self-orthogonal. For the dimension-three codes $C_L(D,(r+1)Q)$ on Hermitian curves over $\F_{r^2}$, $r=2^e\ge4$, we obtain \[ n+2g-r-2\leτ_D(C;Q)\le n+2g-3. \] Consequently the leading genus contribution is asymptotically sharp even in dimension three. On the elliptic curve $y^2+y=x^3$ over $\F_4$, we prove the exact dimension-three threshold $6$ by an explicit multiplier. For repetition codes on the Hermitian family, the threshold equals the general interpolation bound $n+2g-1$. The upper bounds use information sets and hold for $q>3k$, and for $q>2k$ in characteristic two.

papers.title: A Compact Residual-Screened Local Reduced-Order Model for Diffuse-Domain Shape Optimization
papers.abstract: We generalize the compact residual-screened local reduced-order model (CL-ROM) from Brinkman-penalized flow to shape optimization with the diffuse domain method (DDM). As with Brinkman penalization, DDM extends evolving-domain problems to a fixed rectangular domain, allowing one grid for discretization and directly compatible snapshots from different designs. Unlike Brinkman penalization, DDM uses a phase field to weight operators and sources and treats Dirichlet, Neumann and Robin conditions through diffuse boundary terms. The CL-ROM mechanism carries over: recent full-order and corrected solutions determine local reduced spaces, while residual screening, correction with retained factors and objective verification decide when a full-order solve is needed. We derive reduced operators, residuals and sensitivities for each diffuse model, using Galerkin projection for the symmetric problems and least-squares Petrov--Galerkin projection for nonlinear flow. For the symmetric problems we prove a local approximation estimate that admits inexact, corrected snapshots. In numerical tests of shape identification, drag minimization in Navier--Stokes channel flow and compliance minimization of a cantilever, CL-ROM uses reduced solutions for nearly all design updates, reproduces the full-order objectives with relative differences below $5\times10^{-6}$, and is $3.85$ to $7.65$ times faster than a full-order baseline that reuses factorizations as preconditioners.

papers.title: Multiplicity and transverse density as ordering variables of the $Λ/K^0_S$ ratio in oxygen-oxygen collisions at the LHC
papers.abstract: Baryon-to-meson enhancements are commonly compared across collision systems at equal multiplicity. Using published data only, we test whether the $p_T$ dependence of the CMS $Λ/K^0_S$ ratio in minimum-bias O-O collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=5.36$ TeV can be obtained from CMS multiplicity-differential p-Pb and Pb-Pb measurements weighted with the O-O multiplicity distribution. The prediction from p-Pb collisions of equal multiplicity is harder than the data, with a tilt of $+0.35\pm0.04$ in $\ln(\mathrm{prediction}/\mathrm{data})$ versus $\ln p_T$, whereas that from peripheral Pb-Pb collisions is consistent with the data. In a Glauber model calibrated on O-O data, O-O and peripheral Pb-Pb collisions of equal multiplicity have similar transverse densities $ρ=\langle(dN_{ch}/dη)/S_\perp\rangle$, about half of that in p-Pb. Matching the p-Pb reference in $ρ$ instead of multiplicity reduces the tilt by about 60%, to $+0.14\pm0.04$, with nucleons as sources; the tension is fully removed ($-0.02\pm0.04$) only when sub-nucleonic structure is included (three constituents per nucleon), so the conclusion depends on the modeled size of high-multiplicity p-Pb collisions. The published blast-wave velocities of p-Pb and Pb-Pb collisions, which differ at equal multiplicity, are close at equal $ρ$. Multiplicity alone thus does not determine the $Λ/K^0_S$ shape across systems; the data are consistent with a radial boost governed by the transverse density, as expected from hydrodynamics. The same pattern is found in EPOS4, which has a hydrodynamic core, but not in PYTHIA Angantyr. For Ne-Ne collisions, which have the transverse density of O-O at equal multiplicity, the minimum-bias ratio is predicted to agree with O-O within 3-5%, as EPOS4 also predicts.

papers.title: A remark on the compactness of manifolds with non-negative Ricci curvature and uniformly convex boundary
papers.abstract: Yan-Zhu (arXiv:2605.31477) showed the compactness of complete Riemannian manifolds with non-negative Ricci curvature and uniformly convex boundary. In this paper, we give an alternative proof of this compactness theorem.

papers.title: One Assistant, Many Memories: Benchmarking Real-World Group Assistance When Recall Is Not Enough
papers.abstract: The value of memory lies not only in recall but in using it to provide appropriate assistance. Recent benchmarks test memory use in personalisation and agentic tasks, but seldom evaluate assistance without fixed answers or integration across multiple participants. Group chats make both challenges more acute: an assistant must integrate information from multiple members, track revisions and conflicts over time, and produce one response for the group. Yet existing group memory benchmarks rely on synthetic conversations and inherit constrained evaluation from general memory benchmarks, focusing on recall against fixed answers or decisions over a closed set. We introduce GroupAssistBench, the first memory benchmark from real-world group conversations with a deployed group assistant, covering 80,299 messages in 50 groups and costing over $53K. Over the same histories, GroupAssistBench evaluates memory recall (L1) with reference answers and memory use (L2) with service requests without fixed answers across single, distributed, and conflicting memories (M1--M3). Requests are verified to require group history, memories are anchored to their sources, and L2 uses tailored rubrics with penalties derived from real user feedback. Across evaluations of frontier models with full context, retrieval methods, and memory systems, the strongest memory system rivals full context on recall but falls far behind on use, especially for distributed and conflicting memories. Together, two additions that relate retrieved memories and bind remembered facts as response constraints bring consistent gains, showing that group memory systems must improve use, not recall alone.

papers.title: Autonomous cooling of Kerr-cat qubits to minutes-long bit-flip times
papers.abstract: Quantum error correction becomes more hardware efficient when physical noise is strongly biased towards one error channel. Cat qubits realize such a bias by encoding information in two opposite coherent states of a superconducting oscillator, so that bit flips are exponentially suppressed with photon number while phase-flip rates increase only linearly. In Kerr-cat qubits, a driven double-well potential confines these states and enables fast coherent control, but excitations can induce interwell switching, limiting bit-flip times to milliseconds. Here we show that the nonlinear interaction generating the confinement can also cool these excitations. When an intra-well transition becomes resonant with a lossy readout mode, excitations are transferred out of the qubit and dissipated, as established by spectroscopy and relaxation measurements. We observe the predicted exponential scaling of Kerr-cat bit-flip times with photon number, reaching 450 s, over five orders of magnitude beyond previous demonstrations. Phase-flip rates remain consistent with intrinsic photon loss at operating points with seconds-long bit-flip times. We further demonstrate fast Z gates without measurable degradation of bit-flip protection and single-shot readout with a bit-flip probability below $10^{-6}$ per measurement. Autonomous cooling thus brings minutes-long bit-flip protection to Kerr-cat qubits while retaining fast coherent control, without additional cooling drives or circuit elements.

papers.title: Asymptotics for partitions over the Fibonacci numbers and related sequences, II
papers.abstract: In a recent paper of the same title, we considered nondistinct partitions of integers over the Fibonacci sequence and related linearly recurrent sequences. In this paper, continuing this story, we apply the same method, but consider distinct partitions. In particular, let $q_F(m)$ denote the number of ways of writing $m$ as the sum of distinct Fibonacci numbers. It is well-known that, while $q_F(m)$ behaves wildly, its partial sums behave in a more structured way. In particular, Kempton showed that the function $N^{-\log 2/\log\varphi}\sum_{m\leqslant N}q_F(m)$ is asymptotically logarithmically-periodic. In this paper, we improve on this result by providing an explicit error term. Additionally, we prove the analogous result for a class of more general linear recurrent sequences.

papers.title: PrimeSim: A Generalist World Model Simulator from Large-Scale Cross-Embodiment Demonstrations
papers.abstract: A robot world model that serves as a simulator must do more than generate plausible videos: it must faithfully follow commanded actions, maintain consistency across camera views, and sustain coherent long-horizon rollouts. We present PrimeSim, an action-conditioned, multiview world model simulator that addresses these challenges through progressive midtraining and posttraining. Starting from a pretrained video generator, we midtrain on 30,110 hours of robot demonstrations spanning 22 platforms. To improve action following, we introduce a unified cross-embodiment action representation and frame-aligned dual-path conditioning to strengthen action-frame correspondence. To maintain multiview consistency, we develop view-aware interleaved attention with explicit camera identities, enabling cross-view information exchange while preserving view-specific representations. We further introduce a fast-video, slow-memory posttraining framework that transforms the bidirectional video generator into an efficient autoregressive simulator. By combining fast causal generation, self-rollout training, and hierarchical temporal memory, PrimeSim mitigates error accumulation from self-generated histories and supports coherent long-horizon simulation. PrimeSim runs at 10.1 FPS, remains stable over long-horizon rollouts on rigid and deformable manipulation tasks, and transfers to held-out platforms within 100 to 200 gradient steps where the pretrained backbone does not. Against five open-source action-conditioned world models it leads four of the five WorldSimProbe suites and posts the best overall EWMBench score, while fine-grained local calibration still trails the field; its rollouts are faithful enough to support GRPO-based policy optimization. We release the model weights, inference code, and training code.

papers.title: Physics-Based Plausibility Assessment of AI-Predicted Vehicle Parameters for Automotive Radar in Pre-Crash Scenarios
papers.abstract: Automotive radar is a key sensing modality for safety-critical vehicle functions due to its robustness under adverse weather and lighting conditions. Recent advances in AI-based radar perception enable the direct estimation of object parameters from a single radar measurement cycle. However, the internal decision process of data-driven models is typically not explicitly linked to the underlying radar sensing physics. Consequently, object estimates may achieve high statistical accuracy while remaining physically inconsistent with the measured radar signature, particularly in previously unseen scenarios. Such inconsistencies are especially critical for heading estimation, as they directly affect trajectory prediction and collision assessment in pre-crash scenarios. This paper presents a physics-based consistency assessment framework for validating AI-derived vehicle hypotheses in automotive radar perception. The proposed approach generates an expected radar signature from AI-estimated object parameters using a physics-based reference model that incorporates occlusion-dependent edge visibility, aspect- and angle-dependent RCS modeling, and characteristic wheel-induced MD signatures. The expected signature is compared with the observed radar point cloud using a Wasserstein-distance-based consistency metric computed from three complementary features: the spatial distribution of detections along object edges, the local detection count, and the radar reflection intensity. In this way, physically implausible object hypotheses can be identified and corrected independently of the underlying neural network architecture and without model retraining or architectural modifications. The proposed consistency module is integrated as a cascaded post-processing stage for vehicle heading estimation.

papers.title: Conditional Quantum Priors for Chaotic Fluid Dynamics
papers.abstract: Neural networks that predict chaotic dynamics can reproduce short trajectories while misrepresenting statistics over long times. Quantum priors represent selected dynamical statistics through quantum generative models and provide statistical constraints for classical neural networks. Training a separate prior for each value of a system parameter, such as the Reynolds number, does not explicitly model how these statistics vary with that parameter. We learn a conditional quantum prior that approximates selected statistics of an invariant measure at unseen parameter values within the training range, without retraining. For Lorenz-63, the prior reduces mean Jensen-Shannon divergence by 56.9% relative to a classical multilayer perceptron with a comparable number of weights across 96 unseen parameter values. Across 101 values of the same parameter, the shared prior uses 84.7% fewer trainable weights than would be required by a separate quantum neural network at each value. We then use the learned prior to regularize classical neural networks, encouraging their autoregressive rollouts to better reproduce long-term statistics. For Kolmogorov flow at Reynolds number $Re=1000$, prior regularization reduces forecast mean squared error by 66.0% over 318 steps relative to the classical baseline without prior regularization. We also implement a photonic quantum prior for noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices, achieving a mean Jensen-Shannon divergence of $4.58\times10^{-3}$ for Lorenz-63 and $2.59\times10^{-3}$ for Kolmogorov flow at unseen parameter values.

papers.title: Trusting Imagined Futures: Auditing Imagined Rewards for VLA Post-Training
papers.abstract: Video world models enable candidate actions to be evaluated through imagined outcomes, but high predicted rewards can favor trajectories with poor execution quality. We introduce Trusting Imagined Futures (TIF), an offline supervision selection method for vision-language-action (VLA) post-training that audits predicted rewards using execution feedback. A multidimensional reward model predicts a utility score for candidate ranking and five dimensions of execution quality. An auditor uses reward predictions and uncertainty to identify overestimation patterns learned from paired imagined videos and real executions. TIF accepts the candidate with the highest predicted utility when its advantage over the existing trajectory exceeds a margin and its audit risk passes a threshold; otherwise, it retains the existing supervision. The retained real trajectories then supervise behavior cloning. Across four LIBERO suites and three training seeds, TIF achieves a mean success rate of 76.25%, improving over training on the existing trajectories by 3.00 percentage points with the same trajectory count and training budget. Adding audit gating yields 1.47 percentage points with the reward model and advantage margin held fixed. The gains persist against advantage ranking and logistic regression risk selection at matched replacement counts. On recorded videos from three real robot tasks, TIF increases clean completion among selected trajectories from 58.33% to 70.00% across 60 candidate pools.

papers.title: OCR in the Foundation Model Era: From Specialist Models to Unified Models
papers.abstract: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) is among the oldest and most widely deployed applications of artificial intelligence. This survey reviews its development, focusing on the Foundation Model Era. We define OCR through faithful transcription: within a specified visual scope, OCR should completely reconstruct the text, notation, and document structure observable in the source image, and every textual, notational, or structural element in the output must be verifiable from visual evidence in that image. We trace the development from specialist OCR models toward unified models, examining joint text detection and recognition, structured sequence generation, and the use of pretrained vision-language models (VLMs). We organize contemporary OCR systems into five coexisting families: modular toolkits and task-specific models, specialized document VLMs, hybrid workflows, general-purpose VLMs, and commercial products and managed services. We compare their architectures, data, and training, examining hallucination and omission, insufficient spatial grounding, and inference cost in generative OCR. We review evaluation from character and scene text recognition to parsing individual structural elements and full-page transcription, highlighting gaps in consistent output definitions, attribution of performance to individual components, and coverage of real capture conditions and visible content and structure. Finally, we summarize the challenges facing OCR and discuss directions for future research. We continuously track related work at https://github.com/zhihengli-casia/Awesome-OCR-in-the-Foundation-Model-Era.

papers.title: Influence of Geometry and Tissue Damage on the Mechanical Behaviour of Skin Meshing
papers.abstract: Skin meshing increases graft coverage, yet the clinically achieved expansion often falls below the manufacturer's nominal meshing ratio. Previous elastic analyses have demonstrated that mesh topology and skin anisotropy strongly influence graft expansion; however, the effect of progressive damage at larger deformation remains unexplored. This study therefore investigates how progressive damage affects the expansion and mechanical response of skin meshes. The performance of auxetic mesh geometries is compared with conventional Zimmer mesher (ZM) geometry. Human back skin was modelled using a one-term Ogden ground matrix and a Gasser Ogden Holzapfel (GOH) collagen network, with separate scalar Kachanov-type continuum damage variables for each constituent. The auxetic geometries, including 1st- and 2nd-order alternative slits (AS1 and AS2), I-shaped (IS) and H-shaped (HS) re-entrant patterns, and ZM, were analysed with Langer's lines oriented either parallel or perpendicular to the loading direction. Hyperelastic and damage-based formulations were compared up to 25% strain, and the damage-based simulations were subsequently extended to 40% strain. ZM was further loaded to 155% strain; the area ratios attained by HS at 40% strain were matched by ZM at 142.1% and 124.7% strain for Langer's lines parallel and perpendicular to loading, respectively. Results indicate that HS achieves greater coverage than ZM for a given stretch, whereas its damage advantage depends on the orientation of Langer's lines.

papers.title: Leakage-Resilient Computation via Matrix Refreshing
papers.abstract: Leakage-resilient cryptography protects secrets against side-channel attacks, in which a physical implementation reveals partial information about its internal state. A fundamental primitive in this area is a leakage-resilient storage, which allows a secret to be stored in a way that remains secure even if an adversary learns some information about the storage's internal state. A popular approach represents a secret as the inner product of two $n$-bit vectors, called shares. The shares are stored and processed separately by two parts of the implementation, called the left and right parties. Because leakage accumulates over time, the shares must be refreshed repeatedly. We prove that a simple refresh, in which the left party multiplies its share by a uniform invertible matrix $M$ and the right party multiplies its share by $M^{-1}$, is secure under continual local leakage. After $T$ refreshes, each allowing at most $λ$ bits of leakage per party, the transcripts for two stored secrets are at statistical distance at most $C\cdot T\cdot 2^{6λ-n/9}$ for an absolute constant $C$. We also obtain a Boolean-circuit compiler with statistical privacy error at most $C\cdot S\cdot 2^{18λ-n/27}$ for $S$ operations and at most $λ$ bits of local leakage per party per operation. The guarantee covers repeated stateful evaluations with adaptively chosen public inputs, with $S$ counting all operations across invocations. Thus, for polynomial-size circuits, a constant leakage fraction is tolerated with share length depending only on the security parameter. We formalize the refreshing bound, the composition and compiler guarantees, and the expected-work bounds in Lean 4. Our results also provide efficient simulation: the leakage can be reproduced from the public inputs and the circuit outputs alone, with expected polynomial overhead.

papers.title: Sampling Density for Multi-window STFT Phase Retrieval
papers.abstract: We study phase retrieval for multi-window short-time Fourier transforms with windows given by complex linear combinations of the first two normalized Hermite functions. Assume that the family of window coefficient vectors does phase retrieval in $\bbC^2$. We prove that the multi-window magnitude samples uniquely determine every signal in $L^2(\bbR)$ up to a global phase whenever the sampling set is separated with lower Beurling density greater than $2$, or is a translated lattice with density at least $2$. Moreover, we show that the sampling density is the best possible, which improves a result in [P.~Grohs, L.~Liehr, and M.~Rathmair. Multi-window {STFT} phase retrieval: lattice uniqueness, J. Funct. Anal., 288(3): Paper No. 110733, 23, 2025].

papers.title: TraceRouter++: Causal Semantic Routing Realignment via Optimal Transport
papers.abstract: Despite their remarkable capabilities, large foundation models (LFMs) remain susceptible to adversarial manipulation. Current safety intervention methods primarily rely on the \textit{locality hypothesis}, rigidly suppressing isolated neurons or features. However, harmful semantics manifest as distributed, cross-layer circuits, rendering localized ablations both brittle against complex jailbreaks and detrimental to general utility. To bridge this gap, we propose TraceRouter++, a routing-level safety intervention framework that explicitly traces safety-relevant causal routing pathways activated under harmful inputs and realigns their unsafe activation states. Our framework operates in a \textit{Discover-Trace-Realign} paradigm: it first pinpoints a sensitive onset layer via attention divergence and disentangles dense activations into interpretable routing features using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). Subsequently, it maps these features to downstream causal circuits via feature influence scores (FIS). Crucially, departing from rigid suppression paradigms, TraceRouter++ introduces a constrained optimal transport (OT)-based soft routing realignment. By formulating safety intervention as a tractable coordinate-wise marginal optimal transport approximation, our method redirects unsafe activation marginals toward safe-reference marginals within causally identified routing subspaces while preserving non-selected coordinates at the intervention point. This mechanism safely redirects malicious semantic flows while leaving orthogonal computational routes intact. Extensive experiments across representative large language models (LLMs), multimodal large language models (MLLMs), and diffusion models (DMs) show that TraceRouter++ outperforms evaluated baselines, improving adversarial robustness while maintaining a favorable safety-utility trade-off. WARNING: This paper contains unsafe model responses.

papers.title: ScamWorld: An Interactive Environment for Evaluating Web Agents Against Online Fraud
papers.abstract: Web agents increasingly browse, shop, and manage accounts on behalf of their users. Prior work has shown that they can be misled by adversarial content, including prompt injections and deceptive interfaces. Beyond such attacks, agents operating on the open web also encounter online fraud designed to deceive humans, including fraudulent online stores, fake investment platforms, and advance-fee schemes. How web agents respond to such fraud during task execution remains underexplored, in part because scam websites are short-lived, making systematic evaluation difficult. To address this gap, we introduce ScamWorld, an interactive environment that reconstructs reported scam websites across diverse scenarios, fraud mechanisms, and languages. Each reconstructed website reproduces documented fraud mechanisms, making relevant signs of fraud observable before the agent's final action and enabling controlled, repeatable evaluation. Through an extensive study of web agents powered by six frontier LLMs, we find that baseline deception rates range from 11% to 35% across models. Agents proceed more readily with payments than with requests for credentials or wallet information. A closer analysis of agent trajectories shows that some agents acknowledge suspicious conditions yet proceed, at times treating the user's instructions as authorisation to accept additional terms imposed by the website. ScamWorld provides a reusable testbed for systematically evaluating and stress-testing web agents against real-world online fraud.

papers.title: Automaticity of structural defects in fixed points of block substitutions
papers.abstract: We study structural defects in fixed points of block substitutions, building on arXiv:2604.12637 and providing its technical supplement. We develop an automata-based framework to characterize their occurrence and derive verifiable combinatorial criteria. We also introduce simplifications for the construction and analysis of these automata, including tensor-product decompositions, that clarify the mechanisms underlying structural defects and their emergence.

papers.title: From Navier-Stokes to Measure-Valued Euler-Brinkman Equations: Homogenization in the Inviscid Limit
papers.abstract: We study the behaviour of the solution to the Navier-Stokes equations with vanishing viscosity and a no-slip condition in a periodically perforated domain. The behaviour depends on the particle size and the viscosity of the fluid. We prove convergence to a measure-valued solution, provided that the local Reynolds number is small, in the subcritical and critical regime. In the first case, the limit solves the Euler equations, whereas in the second case it solves the Euler-Brinkman equations. This extends the results of https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6544/acfe56 for less regular limit functions. In particular, we also prove existence of measure-valued solutions to the Euler-Brinkman equations, along with weak-strong uniqueness.

papers.title: Splitting of viscosity solutions
papers.abstract: We give a penalization argument for splitting a continuous viscosity solution of two-sided Pucci inequalities into a solution of the same inequalities with zero boundary values and a function satisfying the homogeneous Pucci inequalities and with the same boundary data, settling an open question raised by Silvestre-Sirakov.

papers.title: Reproducibility in open-source RISC-V HW flows
papers.abstract: Open-source hardware is booming. To prevent fragmentation, encourage collaboration and reuse we propose the RISC-V to join forces with Reproducible Builds communities and concentrate innovation potential where its needed most: creation of new micro-architectures, IPs and their integration into new SoCs and applications. To facilitate this goal, we chose Guix, a rigorous solution for reproducible software artefacts. We apply it to dependency management & reproducibility problems in open-source hardware and show the validity of the approach, taking CVA6 as a running example. The end result - a fully reproducible collection of packaged tests, emulation, simulation and cycle-accurate models - shows a promising workflow that could (in future) scale to support larger RISC-V community with reusable software & hardware components for next-generation platforms.

papers.title: Best-of-Many-Worlds MMS Allocation for Chores with Sublinear Disposals
papers.abstract: We study randomized allocations (lotteries) of indivisible chores under additive costs and introduce the notion of MMS1, which requires each agent's bundle to satisfy the maximin share (MMS) bound after the removal of at most one chore. Our main result establishes that every instance admits an ex-ante proportional lottery in whose support every allocation is MMS1 and all but $o(n)$ agents satisfy MMS. Consequently, every realized allocation can be made MMS by disposing of at most $o(n)$ chores. The proposed framework further achieves ex-ante proportionality alongside ex-post $4/3$-MMS, $o(n)$-AMMS, or $1$-out-of-$d$ MMS for $d=(1-o(1))n$. These guarantees substantially improve upon state-of-the-art bounds for MMS allocation for chores with disposal or subsidy, best-of-both-worlds fairness, approximate AMMS, and ordinal MMS approximations.

papers.title: DLER: Dual-Logit Experience Replay for Online Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Online continual learning aims to continuously train neural networks on a non-stationary data stream in a single pass. Rehearsal-based methods alleviate catastrophic forgetting by replaying stored samples, but the imbalance between current and previous data often leads to predictions biased toward current classes. Many approaches have been proposed to overcome the forgetting problem by correcting the bias; however, they still need to be improved in an online fashion. By decomposing the dot-product logits into an angle factor and a norm factor, our analysis reveals that the angle factor efficiently captures novel knowledge but is particularly susceptible to prediction bias, whereas the norm factor helps preserve historical knowledge. Based on these observations, we propose Dual-Logit Experience Replay (DLER), which exploits dual-logits for both model optimization and memory management. Specifically, DLER learns current samples using cosine logits and incorporates additional dot-product logits when replaying previous samples to mitigate prediction bias. To strengthen dual-logit learning under limited replay memory, an auxiliary supervised contrastive objective promotes angular compactness within each class, extending corrections learned from limited replay samples to other samples of the same class. Meanwhile, we introduce a memory update strategy that preferentially retains samples for which dot-product prediction assigns a higher probability to the correct class than cosine prediction, aligning sample selection with dual-logit training. Extensive experiments on three datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of DLER, particularly under limited memory budgets.

papers.title: Modelling lock-in of AI adoption through skill erosion
papers.abstract: Generative AI can improve immediate performance but may erode the human skills required for future work. We study a model in which individuals tend to imitate successful peers, while their independent skills grow with practice and erode with reliance on AI. Because each agent's skill reflects their history, non-users and AI users develop different skill distributions, which we derive exactly. Skill erosion can produce bistability and hysteresis between a low-adoption, high-skill state and a high-adoption, low-skill state. When agents rarely change behaviour at random, the two transitions are asymmetric. A single AI user spreads through a population of experts only if AI-assisted work earns more than expert work, whatever the timescale of skill adaptation. A single non-user, by contrast, can lead an AI-dependent population back to independent work only if they regain enough skill before returning to AI, which becomes easier the more persistent behaviours are. As AI improves, adoption can jump abruptly, and a sufficiently long increase in its benefit, such as a period of low prices, can leave a population relying on AI after the benefit has returned to its initial value. Skill erosion thus creates a history-dependent switching cost that can make widespread AI adoption difficult to reverse.

papers.title: FourSight: Stable FP4 RL Post-Training via Sequence Filtering and Sparse Channel Compensation
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training increasingly targets low-bit deployment, with NVFP4 weight-and activation quantization (W4A4) becoming the state-of-the-practice format. However, integrating NVFP4 into RL degrades rollout quality and amplifies cross-engine training-inference mismatch (TIM), destabilizing training. We show that these failures are concentrated rather than uniform - severely mismatched tail tokens concentrate in a few outlier sequences, while policy weights remain largely intact and quantization error concentrates in a few high-variance activation channels. Guided by this, we present FourSight, an algorithm-system co-design with two targeted solutions: TIM-aware sequence filtering that excludes drifted trajectories from policy updates, and sparse precision compensation that keeps only top-variance channels in BF16 while retaining native NVFP4 elsewhere. We further design a fused SpliceGEMM kernel with specialized prefill and decode datapaths to minimize overhead. FourSight sustains near-BF16 accuracy and strong FP4 deployment quality across models and engines, while improving step-to-accuracy by 1.76-2.60x and staying within 2.3% of FP4 step time up to 120B-scale models.

papers.title: Sufficient and Necessary Smooth Barrier-Like Conditions for Continuous-Time Finite-Horizon Safety Verification
papers.abstract: We study finite-horizon safety verification for continuous-time stochastic systems modeled by stochastic differential equations. Given an open and bounded safe set, a compact initial set, a finite time horizon, and a prescribed violation-probability threshold, the objective is to certify that the exit probability from the safe set before the horizon remains below the threshold. Under uniform ellipticity of the diffusion matrix and regularity of the safe-set boundary, we develop a time-dependent barrier-like condition expressed as a set of functional inequalities, obtained by relaxing a parabolic initial-boundary value problem associated with the exit probability. If a function satisfies the condition, then the probability of leaving the safe set before the horizon is guaranteed to remain below the threshold. Conversely, when the exit probability is strictly smaller than the prescribed threshold uniformly over the initial set, the barrier-like condition is also necessary: there exists a smooth function satisfying it. Furthermore, when the dynamics are polynomial and the set descriptions are semialgebraic, the problem of verifying the condition admits a sum-of-squares formulation that is both sound and complete, yielding a complete degree hierarchy for finite-horizon stochastic safety verification.

papers.title: NP-Hardness and a PTAS for Maximum Interval Multicover, with Applications to Dense Subgraphs
papers.abstract: Given intervals and points on a line, each point with a demand, and a budget $K$, Maximum Interval Multicover asks for at most $K$ intervals that satisfy as many points as possible, a point being satisfied if it lies in at least as many chosen intervals as its demand. One application is committee elections in which each candidate is approved by consecutive voters and voters have individual demands. Xu, Ran and Zhang introduced the problem and gave a $1/2$-approximation; the objective is not submodular when demands exceed one. Li, Tu, Zhang and Cao gave a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for the minimization counterpart, unweighted partial interval multicover, and asked for its complexity. We prove that both problems are NP-hard, even for intervals of equal length; as their optima are integers bounded by the input size, neither has a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$. We then give a PTAS for Maximum Interval Multicover, also for arbitrary nonnegative nondecreasing rewards for the coverage of each point. Building on a decomposition from Nonner's PTAS for Densest $k$-Subgraph on interval graphs, our scheme cuts the line into pieces at a small loss and solves every piece exactly. The key dynamic program handles intervals crossing a common point by choosing an interleaving of their left and right endpoints rather than sweeping along the line; it needs only two counters to track these intervals. The same algorithm yields PTASes on convex bipartite graphs for Bipartite Dense Subgraph, improving on the ratio $2/3$ of Backer and Keil for the subclass of bipartite permutation graphs, and on interval graphs for Maximum $k$-Vertex Cover and weighted clique counts.

papers.title: DAMA/LIBRA dark matter signal: a global analysis
papers.abstract: The annual modulation reported by the DAMA/LIBRA collaboration remains in tension with the null results of other direct-detection experiments. We investigate the compatibility of DAMA/LIBRA with LZ, PICO-60 and CDMSlite within a generalized non-relativistic effective field theory (EFT) framework. In addition to the EFT operator expansion we investigate additional modifications to the standard WIMP picture, including inelastic scattering, variations in the NaI quenching factors, and a rescaling of the dark-matter velocity dispersion. We perform a Markov chain Monte Carlo analysis in this extended model space, using two alternative approaches to the likelihood function describing the DAMA/LIBRA data. Both approaches result in strong discrepancy between the data from DAMA/LIBRA and other experiments. We conclude that the extended model space considered here cannot accommodate the DAMA/LIBRA signal while remaining consistent with the non-observation of dark matter in other experiments.

papers.title: Separately continuous maps into regular spaces and continuity of operations in separable semitopological groups
papers.abstract: A space is feebly compact if every locally finite family of nonempty open subsets of it is finite; a Tychonoff space is feebly compact if and only if it is pseudocompact. M. Tkachenko asked whether a regular feebly compact semitopological group is a topological group provided that it is separable, has countable tightness, or is a $k$-space; for Tychonoff groups the answer is known to be positive. We answer this question in the separable case: every regular separable feebly compact semitopological group is a topological group. The proof is based on the following result: if $X$ is a separable Baire space, $Y$ is a feebly compact space and $Z$ is a regular space, then every separately continuous map $X\times Y\to Z$ is strongly quasicontinuous. Unlike the known approaches for Tychonoff spaces, the proof does not use real-valued functions. More generally, every regular separable semitopological group which is $Γ^{BM}_o$-nonmeager, a Baire-type property defined by a modification of the Banach-Mazur game, is a topological group. This class of groups contains all regular separable Baire groups which are feebly $p$-spaces; feebly $p$-spaces form a wider class of spaces, which contains all feebly compact spaces and all $p$-spaces. The results remain valid for spaces satisfying the assumptions locally. In particular, every regular locally separable locally feebly compact semitopological group is a topological group.

papers.title: A Multidimensional Evaluation Framework for Artificial Intelligence-Based Ocean State Forecasts
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) based ocean state forecasts now approach or surpass those produced by operational ocean forecasting systems as measured by conventional pointwise metrics. However, these metrics may favor spatially smoothed forecasts and cannot determine whether forecast variables remain physically coherent. Forecast evaluation should therefore move beyond overall pointwise accuracy toward assessing forecast trustworthiness. We propose a multidimensional framework comprising overall pointwise accuracy, physical consistency, and distributional consistency. Overall pointwise accuracy summarizes forecast and reference agreement over all valid samples; physical consistency evaluates dynamical balances using model outputs alone; and distributional consistency evaluates distribution tails and multiscale spatial structures. Three AI models were deployed as representative testbeds in a unified operational environment. This comprehensive assessment shows that lower overall pointwise errors cannot preclude substantial dynamical imbalances and suppressed fine-scale variance. Conversely, higher pointwise errors may arise from spatial displacement of coherent structures rather than a poor representation of their amplitude. The results demonstrate that the evaluation of AI ocean forecasting models should be based on the multi-dimensional assessment of forecast trustworthiness, rather than solely relying on a single metric. The study provides a preliminary framework for AI model intercomparison, which is also informative for targeted model refinement and operational implementation.

papers.title: Fault-tolerant shallow recurrent decoders for sparse sensing with missing sensor measurements
papers.abstract: Real-world sensing systems are inherently imperfect: sensors may fail, intermittently disconnect, operate with asynchronous sampling rates, and be subject to noise, leading to measurement streams that are irregular, incomplete, and heterogeneous. Nevertheless, sensing strategies for real-time state reconstruction typically assume synchronous and continuously active sensors, a constraint that substantially limits their applicability in operational environments. In this work, we introduce fault-tolerant sparse sensing strategies in the context of shallow recurrent decoders (SHRED) to enable high-dimensional state estimation from sparse, asynchronous, and missing sensor measurements. Specifically, we consider naive imputation strategies, fault-tolerant recurrent temporal encoders, and we introduce four different transformer-based masking mechanisms to make SHRED explicitly aware of sensor availability through the binary data-availability mask. Moreover, we further introduce a multi-step decoding training objective for SHRED, resulting in smoother latent trajectories and more robust predictions. Throughout a synthetic benchmark and three real-world problems in hydrodynamic and ocean modeling, we show that (i) transformer-based masking mechanisms outperform standard imputation techniques and fault-tolerant recurrent architectures, (ii) the multi-step decoding training objective enhances reconstruction fidelity and robustness in the presence of heterogeneous missing-data patterns, while (iii) the computational efficiency of SHRED is preserved, with no additional inference-time overhead.

papers.title: VisSearch-Bench: Evaluating Long Horizon Visual Search in Multimodal Agents
papers.abstract: Multimodal agents use web and image tools to answer questions beyond their internal knowledge. Some search tasks use images mainly to identify an initial entity, then rely on text retrieval. These tasks offer limited insight into how agents connect information across images, objects, and search steps. We therefore focus on visual context management. This involves organizing and using visual information and linking it to other findings during search. Visually intensive tasks require agents to combine object appearance, local details, or spatial relations with external information. We introduce VisSearch-Bench, with 204 human-written tasks across 7 main domains and 25 subdomains. It covers Set-wise Visual Search, Sequential Visual Search, Hybrid Wide-Deep Search, Competitive Visual Disambiguation, and Visual-Structure-Guided Search. Each task provides a reference answer, traceable evidence, and scoring rules. Accuracy measures complete task success, while Process Score measures the correctness and completeness of individual results and subquestion answers. Across 16 multimodal models, the best system fully solves only 26.47% of tasks, even with search tools. These results highlight the challenge of linking visual evidence with search results to produce complete answers.

papers.title: Quantum sensing of a weak drive signal in cascaded quantum van der Pol oscillators
papers.abstract: We have constructed a quantum sensing system composed of two quantum van der Pol (vdP) oscillators. Coherent and dissipative couplings are combined to establish a generic nonreciprocal coupling between the two vdP subsystems. A weak driving signal to be measured is applied to an oscillator (probe system) and then transferred via non-reciprocal coupling to another oscillator (measurement system) that is easier to measure. This allows for the acquisition of information about the driving strength of the signal being measured. For the classic cascaded dual vdP oscillators, complete non-reciprocal coupling yields a much higher susceptibility than a single classical vdP oscillator alone. For the quantum vdP system, the sensitivity generally does not diverge at the zero driving force point. When only dissipative coupling and two-particle loss are present, the system will have a dark mode at the zero driving force point, which enables the measurement precision to ultimately reach the Heisenberg limit in the time domain. Enhancing incoherent driving can effectively resist dissipation and thereby improve measurement precision. Moreover, in the strong incoherent driving regime, the improvement factor of non-reciprocal coupling over reciprocal coupling in terms of measurement precision tends to infinity as the two-particle loss rate of the measurement system approaches zero.

papers.title: On the Convexity of Common Resource Adequacy and Capacity Accreditation Metrics
papers.abstract: Many emerging capacity expansion optimization formulations implicitly presume the convexity (or concavity) of power system adequacy risk (or capacity accreditation) metrics. These assumptions have yet to be formally justified. We present concise mathematical proofs validating the claim for certain metrics (expected unserved energy and effective load carrying capability), but also provide simple invalidating counterexamples for others (loss-of-load expectation and equivalent firm capacity). Formulations built on non-convex (non-concave) metrics structurally undervalue candidate portfolio adequacy, and so cannot claim to produce least-cost expansion plans.

papers.title: TapeSAC: Automated, Pareto-Optimal Fine-Grained Memory Management for Large Model Training
papers.abstract: Selective activation checkpointing (SAC) decides which activations to save for the backward pass and which to recompute: each choice is a point in the plane of peak memory and recomputation time, and the goal is that plane's Pareto frontier. Current practice falls short of this goal. Hand-tuned policies fix a single point that does not adapt when the model, batch or kernels change; PyTorch's SAC reruns each block's forward pass in program order, recomputing values the backward pass never reads; and the memory budget of torch.compile treats recomputation as free or forbidden and selects saved tensors by bytes alone, an assumption that fails for the custom kernels that produce many of a large model's activations. We present TapeSAC, which automates SAC in eager PyTorch without editing the model's forward code. TapeSAC records each block's forward pass at the dispatcher and, during backward, replays only the producers of the values autograd consumes, so saving a tensor eliminates every producer needed only for it. A planner selects the saved tensors from measured recomputation costs under a single limit on step-peak memory. On Qwen3.8-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, replay alone reduces step time by 3.0% and 1.7% versus full checkpointing at no greater memory cost; memory-aware planning raises these gains to 6.3% and 13.9% under a 90%-of-device-memory limit. The evaluated hand-tuned policies fall short of this memory-recomputation frontier and, on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, run out of memory at larger batches. Over 500 steps on real data, TapeSAC reduces training time by 8-11%; on Qwen3.5-397B, it is 2.7% faster than a model-specific hand-tuned policy while using 14% less memory.

papers.title: Local Distributed Computation under Crash Failures
papers.abstract: We study deterministic algorithms for locally checkable graph problems in the synchronous LOCAL model with crash failures, where a crashing node may send messages to only some neighbors. We introduce consistent neighborhoods: partial radius-$R$ views that agree locally across surviving edges and are complete without crashes. For $R=T+\ell+1$, these views allow local simulation of $T$-round fault-free algorithms that remain correct on subgraphs, satisfying constraints wherever the radius-$\ell$ checking neighborhood contains no crash. On graphs with at most $n$ nodes and maximum degree at most $Δ\geq3$, we construct these views in $O(\min\{n,(Δ-1)^R,RΔf\})$ rounds when a crash bound $f\geq1$ is globally known; the first two bounds require no knowledge of $f$. For $Δ=2$ or girth greater than $2R$, including forests, $O(R)$ rounds suffice. Our upper bounds are essentially tight in suitable parameter regimes. One crash can force $Ω(n)$ rounds even for $R=3$ on diameter-two graphs. For each fixed $Δ\geq3$ and sufficiently large $R$, we prove a $(Δ-1)^{R-O(\sqrt R)}$ lower bound even with crashes restricted to round beginnings. We also prove an $Ω(ΔRf)$ lower bound when $R\geq4\lceil\log_{Δ-1}f\rceil+4$ and $n\geqΔRf$. For locally checkable labeling (LCL) problems, we preserve $O(\log^* n)$ complexity under any number of crashes whenever this bound holds without faults on all graphs with a fixed degree bound. In contrast, we construct an LCL on graphs of maximum degree at most five with fault-free complexity $Θ(\log n)$ and crash-tolerant complexity $Θ(n)$. Finally, any fault-free sinkless-orientation algorithm can be transformed to tolerate any number of crashes with only one additional round, guaranteeing correctness even at surviving nodes adjacent to crashes.

papers.title: Knowledge Graph Lakehouse: A Cloud-Native Architecture for Managing Enterprise Knowledge Graphs at Scale
papers.abstract: Modern data architectures for integrating heterogeneous data sources to discover actionable knowledge include the data warehouse, the data lake, and the data lakehouse, which combines the flexibility of the data lake with the structured data management capabilities of the data warehouse through metadata, indexes, and caching. Enterprise knowledge graphs (KGs) offer an alternative approach to such integration for the purposes of data analysis, but handling them at scale must address the Three Vs of big data: volume, velocity, and variety. Contextualized KGs (CKGs) meet part of that challenge by enriching facts with contextual information, yet many applications require only a context-specific subset of that knowledge. We propose the Knowledge Graph Lakehouse (KG Lakehouse), a cloud-native microservice architecture that adapts the data lakehouse paradigm for management of CKGs at scale. The KG Lakehouse indexes incoming source documents along configurable context dimensions and stores these documents in a data lake, from which application-specific CKGs are constructed on demand instead of maintaining a single, monolithic KG. We realize the proposed architecture as a proof of concept, with independently deployable services built from established cloud technology; context dimensions and format-specific document handling enter as configuration, leaving the architecture independent of the application domain. We evaluate the implemented system in experiments on a distributed cluster deployment.

papers.title: The Power of Bidegeneracy for Hypergraph Data Structures
papers.abstract: A hypergraph $H = (V,E)$ describes a set system over a vertex universe $V$. Hypergraphs are increasingly popular in network science, as they represent interactions between subsets of vertices. A natural challenge is to design a data structure for $H$ to quickly answer basic questions about it, e.g. how many neighbors a vertex $v$ has or whether a hyperedge contains a vertex subset $S$. Such questions are trivial for graphs, for which we simply inspect the adjacency list. The gold standard, from a data structures perspective, would be near-linear time preprocessing and query answering in (poly)logarithmic time. Since this is unlikely for arbitrary $H$, we ask for well-motivated hypergraph properties that can make such a goal possible. We introduce bidegeneracy, a measure of hypergraph sparsity that strictly generalizes many other measures, including bounded degree, bounded rank, and bounded $\infty$-degeneracy. We show that bounded bidegeneracy yields fast hypergraph data structures. For a large set of fundamental queries, including their listing and sampling versions, we obtain near-linear preprocessing and (poly)logarithmic query time. Moreover, direct reductions from assumptions like the Orthogonal Vectors Conjecture suggest that, without assumptions on the input, these structures require almost-quadratic preprocessing or almost-linear query time. We use bidegeneracy to compute a compressed representation of $H$ and perform careful reductions to stabbing and searching problems in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Our framework significantly extends the well-studied "partial matching" problem of finding database entries through wildcard search. It also uncovers an intriguing connection between hypergraph sparsity, compression, and the complexity of hypergraph primitives. We also find remarkably low bidegeneracy in hypergraph datasets from the literature, suggesting practical consequences.

papers.title: Near-Linear Lower Bounds for Testing Directed Acyclicity
papers.abstract: We study testing acyclicity of directed graphs in the bounded-degree incidence-lists model, where a tester can query the outneighbors of a vertex but not its inneighbors. Despite significant effort, no tester with $o(n)$ queries is known, while the best established lower bounds are $\widetildeΩ(n^{5/9})$ for one-sided testers (Chen, Randolph, Servedio, and Sun, 2022) and $Ω(n^{1/3})$ for two-sided testers (Bender and Ron, 2002). We show that a query exponent arbitrarily close to one is necessary: for every fixed $η\in(0,1)$, there exists a constant $\varepsilon_η>0$ such that, for every constant $d\ge2$, every randomized adaptive two-sided $\varepsilon_η$-tester for acyclicity of simple $n$-vertex directed graphs whose indegrees and outdegrees are at most $d$ makes $Ω(n^{1-η})$ queries. Our proof overcomes two barriers. First, in previous constructions, the acyclic part of the graph is easy to recognize, which helps an algorithm stay inside the cyclic part. We hide a high-girth cyclic core inside a hierarchy of acyclic masking regions, in which each region imitates the levels below it and can be told apart from them only through rare events, and an iterated information-theoretic argument shows that every exploration observes only small, low-diameter forest components of the core. Second, a two-sided tester may exploit the statistics of collisions without ever seeing a cycle, and at a near-linear budget collisions are unavoidable. We compare complete transcripts with those of an acyclic input built on a fixed core by counting injective embeddings of the observed forest: in high-girth cores, all connected collision patterns of bounded order contribute identically, which makes the two transcript distributions statistically indistinguishable.

papers.title: Attending to Memory Writes Reduces Seed Variability in Recurrent Length Generalization
papers.abstract: Recurrent memory requires learning useful updates, but attention added to assist learning can also compromise length generalization. We study bounded delta attention: causal attention over uncorrected update proposals whose bounded correction enters the recurrent update. Its implementation in TraceRelay combines additive phase recurrence with attention computed before a parallel scan. On prefix-supervised modulo-5, trained at lengths 1--40, three findings characterize its behavior at length 80. First, upper delta attention attains $70.81\pm8.26$% accuracy across seven seeds, versus $69.21\pm22.42$% for the local-attention recurrent baseline (mean $\pm$ sample SD): a 63.2% reduction in SD with a similar mean. Upper state attention also reduces variation, reaching $74.75\pm6.24$%, so this benefit is not unique to update-level attention. Disabling the upper delta correction retains $70.62\pm8.60$%. Second, blocking gradients at the delta-attention inputs changes accuracy to $65.25\pm12.40$% in the matched seven-seed comparison, increasing SD by 50.2%. It also delays a 99% validation threshold on average among the same six seeds that reach it; the 95% threshold is reached earlier on average with input-gradient blocking across all seven seeds. Third, lower delta attention exhibits substantially less extrapolation degradation than lower state attention: 62.60% versus 19.40%, against a 71.06% baseline. Removing its correction reduces accuracy to 22.56%; its advantage over lower state attention also persists under input-gradient blocking. These observations motivate bounded update-level attention as a recurrent learning scaffold, combining reduced seed variation with less severe degradation in a placement where state attention fails.

papers.title: Heads That Write, Not Just Point: Image Retrieval Heads in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) can process interleaved text and multiple images in a single context, but how they internally identify the image relevant to a question remains poorly understood. We study this grounding step as in-context image retrieval and introduce ICIR-MCQ, a controlled probe for head-level analysis of image retrieval. Using each head's attention mass over image-token spans, we first identify sparse pointer heads that reliably point to the target image. These heads transfer beyond the probe: a single pointer head is competitive with external vision-language retrievers on a naturalistic multi-image retrieval benchmark, showing that LVLMs contain a strong internal image retrieval signal. Attention alone, however, shows where a head reads from, not what its output passes on to later layers, so we introduce a complementary output-side analysis. For each head, we train a lightweight image retriever on its value-weighted output and use it to identify writer heads, whose outputs contain enough information to identify the target image. Surprisingly, the pointer and writer criteria select substantially different head sets, with only 35 to 47 heads overlapping among the top-100 heads under each criterion. Targeted set-partition ablations show that the heads most important for standard multi-image inference are concentrated in this pointer-writer intersection, while heads selected by only one criterion show less consistent separation from random-head controls. The most consistent causal effects arise from heads selected by both the attention-based pointer and output-side writer criteria. Code and data: https://github.com/parkquasar/Image-Retrieval-Heads.

papers.title: Search for heavy neutral leptons in top quark decays with same-sign, same-flavor dilepton final states in proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV
papers.abstract: A search for a Majorana-type heavy neutral lepton (HNL) produced in top quark decays is reported. The search is based on proton-proton collision data at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 138 fb$^{-1}$, collected during 2016$-$2018 with the CMS detector at the CERN LHC. In the type-I seesaw model, a Majorana HNL can mediate lepton-number-violating top quark decays. The search targets top quark pair production events in which one top quark decays into a bottom quark and a W boson, which subsequently decays into a charged lepton (electron or muon) and an HNL. The Majorana HNL then decays into a W boson and a charged lepton with the same sign and flavor as the one produced with the HNL. The experimental signature features a same-sign, same-flavor lepton pair and jets. The HNL masses between 20 and 100 GeV are probed. The data agree with the standard model background prediction. Observed (expected) upper limits at 95% confidence level are set on the branching fraction of the top quark decay into an HNL, a charged lepton, and a bottom quark, varying between [1.1 (0.71)] $\times$10$^{-5}$ and [4.8 (3.0)] $\times$10$^{-5}$ in the dielectron channel, and between [3.7 (3.4)] $\times$10$^{-6}$ and [2.4 (1.3)] $\times$10$^{-5}$ in the dimuon channel.

papers.title: GAMA-23 deep field with uGMRT Band-2: source catalogue and source count
papers.abstract: We present the low-frequency GAMA-23 field of the Galaxy and Mass Assembly (GAMA) survey with upgraded Giant Meterwave Radio Telescope (uGMRT) observations in Band-2 ($120-250$ MHz). The on-source observation was conducted for ${\sim}5$ hours. The final image achieved an off-source RMS noise of 320 $μ$Jy beam$^{-1}$, covering an area of $5.86\,\text{deg}^2$ with restoring beam size of $15.4''{\times}8.2''$ at the central frequency of 183 MHz. The catalogue derived from the radio image includes 569 sources with a flux density limit of ${\geq}\,5σ$. The flux density measurements and the positional accuracy are cross-verified and compared with other radio catalogues available in the literature. The spectral indices derived from fitting a power law are -0.68$^{+0.18}_{-0.23}$ for the ASKAP EMU catalogue and -0.72$^{+0.19}_{-0.24}$ for the NVSS catalogue. The normalised source count derived from this catalogue is consistent with models and observations with a nominal catalogue threshold of 1.7 mJy, while the sensitivity varies across the image.

papers.title: Modeling runaway electron mitigation via passively driven plasma instabilities in a high-current tokamak
papers.abstract: A critical challenge for tokamak-based fusion power plants is the formation of high-current, relativistic runaway electron (RE) beams during abrupt confinement loss events called disruptions. RE beams may significantly damage machine components if left unmitigated, jeopardizing the operational and economic viability of fusion power plants. We present the first self-consistent extended magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) computational study of RE mitigation with a passively driven RE mitigation coil (REMC) in a high-current tokamak. RE generation and transport are coupled with REMC-driven MHD activity in a 3D simulation that models the thermal and current quench phases of a mid-plane disruption, together with the vertical displacement and final termination of the plasma and RE beam on SPARC -- a high-field, high-current tokamak designed to achieve a fusion gain Q > 1. We demonstrate that REMC-driven magnetic stochasticity can reduce the RE current by over an order-of-magnitude when compared to unmitigated disruptions. The final termination is mediated via a post-thermal-quench "cold" vertical displacement of the plasma, which, together with magnetic stochasticity, increases RE losses via scrape-off once the plasma contacts the first wall. These results demonstrate a viable mechanism for RE mitigation using passively driven plasma instabilities on high-current tokamaks.

papers.title: Cool Graphs: Active Property Search Towards Quantum Nano-Refrigerators
papers.abstract: Nanodevices that absorb energy from their thermal environment can act as quantum refrigerators. Finding suitable configurations, however, is a needle-in-a-haystack problem: the many-body state space scales exponentially with the size of the device, where each candidate configuration requires an expensive quantum-chemical computation. We introduce a search framework that couples a Graph Variational Autoencoder (GVAE) with an uncertainty-driven Active Learning (AL) loop to efficiently identify energy-absorbing configurations in electronic junctions with a 2D "working material" to be optimized. The GVAE maps physical parameters - site energies, coupling matrices, temperature - into a smooth latent space that distinguishes cooling from dissipative parameter regimes, achieving a classification discriminability of $0.920 \pm 0.004$ on held-out configurations and $0.895 \pm 0.010$ on unseen extrapolation topologies. An AL pipeline based on Monte Carlo dropout then targets the decision boundary, iteratively selecting the candidates where the model is least certain for simulation. Over 32 AL cycles, the uncertainty-driven strategy discovers energy absorbing systems at rates consistently exceeding the random baseline across all tested topologies (where only 1.9-8.4% of configurations exhibit the desired property), providing a data-efficient pathway for navigating a combinatorically large design space. The learned latent space organizes configurations along physically interpretable axes, that correlate with underlying microscopic model parameters. This hints at the existence of "cooling coordinates" - low-dimensional, physically interpretable quantities separating cooling from non-cooling regimes. Our framework, thus, paves a new way towards effective cooling of nanoscale electronic information processing devices, to reduce the environmental footprint of high performance computing.

papers.title: Exponential decay for the two-dimensional Heisenberg model
papers.abstract: In this work, we prove exponential decay for the spin correlation of the spin $O(\mathsf{N})$ model for $\mathsf{N}\geq3$ at every inverse temperature $ β>0 $. In particular, our work confirms Polyakov's prediction in 1975 on the Heisenberg model, i.e., the case of $\mathsf{N}=3$. To this end, we investigate a generalized $O(\mathsf{N})$ model where $ \mathsf{N} $ is a positive \emph{real number}, as follows: we sample a loop soup on the metric graph (say of a box) with intensity $ \tfrac{\mathsf{N}}{2} $ subject to the conditioning that the local time at each lattice vertex is $β$, and then for each loop we independently assign it to copies $1\leq \mathsf{i}\leq \lceil\mathsf{N}\rceil$ such that it is assigned to copy $\mathsf{i}$ with probability $ \tfrac{1}{\mathsf{N}} $ for $ 1\leq \mathsf{i}\leq \lfloor\mathsf{N}\rfloor $. Then, by Lupu's isomorphism theorem, we can construct a spin field by assigning a random sign to each loop soup cluster in each copy independently, such that the field coincides with the spin $O(\mathsf{N})$ model when $\mathsf{N}$ is an integer. We then establish exponential decay for every real-valued $\mathsf{N}>2$. Our result reveals an underlying mechanism for exponential decay, which emerges as soon as $\mathsf{N}>2$ (i.e., as soon as beyond the range of the XY model) and does not necessarily rely on the rotation symmetry in the sphere $ \mathbb{S}^{2} $.

papers.title: Fast verification of fault tolerant magic state preparation circuits with the CNOT + T gate set
papers.abstract: Magic state preparation is often among the most expensive operations in a fault tolerant quantum computation. One obstacle to coming up with better magic state preparation circuits lies in verifying their fault tolerance properties, as it is difficult to verify either by hand or in software that a very large number of combinations of faults do not give rise to high-weight or logical errors, especially in a non-Clifford circuit. In this work, we propose the use of the CNOT + T gate set to fault-tolerantly prepare a large class of magic states. We consider the propagation of Pauli faults within CNOT + T circuits and derive properties similar to those of Pauli faults within Clifford circuits, with a view to verifying fault tolerance as efficiently as possible. We present Comb, a library that can verify the fault tolerance of CNOT + T magic state preparation circuits, and demonstrate its use in verifying the fault tolerance of distance three and distance five magic state preparation circuits in minutes on a laptop. We present a distance five magic state preparation circuit that was discovered using Comb. As an independent confirmation of Comb's correctness we compare its findings to circuit-level noisy simulations for several magic state preparation circuits.

papers.title: Next-to-leading order QCD corrections to fully charm tetraquark radiative decays
papers.abstract: We present the first complete next-to-leading-order (NLO) QCD calculation of the fully charm tetraquark radiative decays $T_{4c}(0^{++},2^{++})\toγJ/ψ$ and $T_{4c}(1^{+-})\toγη_c$ at leading order in the relative velocity. The NLO widths are $2.3$--$3.1$ times the leading-order (LO) widths for the long-distance matrix element (LDME) inputs considered here, with $m_c=1.5$ GeV and $μ_R=2m_c$. In the scalar channel, the NLO corrections change the relative contributions of the two color-spin components and their interference. For the tensor channel, the longitudinal fraction $f_L$ of the daughter $J/ψ$ changes from $0.11$ at LO to $0.18$ at strictly expanded NLO, with sensitivity to higher-order corrections. These NLO results provide valuable theoretical input for searches for states predicted below their respective lowest dicharmonium thresholds and for probing the spin and short-distance structure of observed tetraquark candidates.

papers.title: Hereditarily Lindelöf and hereditarily separable subspaces of function spaces
papers.abstract: A space is ESLC if it contains neither an $S$-space nor an $L$-space, and NFS is the class of spaces containing no free sequences of length $ω_1$. We prove that under $\mathrm{MA}(ω_1)$, if all finite powers of $X$ belong to NFS, then $C_p(X)^ω$ is ESLC; thus, for subspaces of $C_p(X)$, hereditary Lindelöfness, hereditary separability and countable spread coincide. This is derived from a dual form of a theorem of Todorčević. A Lindelöf $Σ$-space belongs to NFS if and only if its compact subspaces have countable tightness. Hence $C_p(X)$ contains no $L$-spaces if $X$ is a Lindelöf $Σ$-space of countable tightness and $\mathrm{MA}(ω_1)$ holds, or if $X$ is any Lindelöf $Σ$-space and PFA holds. Under $\mathrm{MA}(ω_1)$, all iterated function spaces of Corson compact spaces are ESLC, and in ZFC the space $C_p(X,\{0,1\})$ is ESLC for every zero-dimensional Corson compact space $X$.

papers.title: MiCaDe: Online LiDAR-Camera Miscalibration Change Detection for Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Reliable multi-sensor perception in autonomous vehicles requires accurate calibration between cameras and LiDAR. However, calibration drift is often unavoidable in long-term deployments: vibrations, thermal effects, and minor mechanical shocks may alter the relative pose between sensors, leading to systematic errors in downstream fusion tasks. We propose MiCaDe (Miscalibration Change Detection), an online solution detecting when the extrinsic LiDAR-camera calibration parameters are no longer accurate by means of sequential change detection. MiCaDe requires no calibration targets, or modification of the perception stack, providing low false-alarm rates with negligible computational overhead. Our key insight is that 3D and 2D bounding boxes produced by standard object detectors should remain geometrically consistent under correct calibration. By matching cross-modal detections, we derive geometric consistency metrics that serve as sensitive indicators of extrinsic drift. These metrics are aggregated into fixed-size batches and scored against a reference distribution, producing a likelihood stream that is monitored by a Change Point Model (CPM). Crucially, the CPM accumulates statistical evidence over time, enabling detection of subtle drifts that would otherwise go unnoticed. Experiments on multiple long-sequence datasets and on a real-world dataset with physically induced miscalibration confirm reliable detection under diverse conditions. Code available at: https://github.com/CarloSgaravatti/MiCaDe.

papers.title: EP-LVMQA: Evidence-Preserving Coarse-to-Fine Localization for Low-Quality Long Video Moment Question Answering
papers.abstract: Long instructional videos are increasingly used in medical education, industrial training, and procedural knowledge transfer, yet their evidence is often incomplete or unreliable: subtitles may be missing, ASR noisy, OCR sparse, and decisive actions briefly shown without narration. Existing VideoQA systems typically return labels or free-form text, making answer support difficult to inspect. We study Long Video Moment Question Answering (LVMQA), where a system returns timestamped answer-supporting evidence. We propose EP-LVMQA, an evidence-preserving coarse-to-fine framework comprising an Uncertainty-Aware Multimodal Evidence Timeline, a Coarse Evidence Planner, and an Evidence-Conditioned Fine Localizer. An evidence card transfers planner scores, matched cues, source-confidence proxies, modality-specific evidence, neighboring context, and a temporal prior between the latter two modules. On MedVidQA, EP-LVMQA achieves 26.1 R1@0.5 and 31.8 mIoU, improving the strongest non-ours results by 6.3 and 5.1 points. It raises Suff.@2 and Ver.@2 to 25.4 and 22.6, gains of 9.5 and 8.8 points. Under matched low-quality perturbations, average relative degradation is reduced from the strongest non-ours value of 14.6% to 11.1%. On Ego4D-NLQ and QVHighlights, EP-LVMQA remains broadly comparable to established task-specific localization methods.

papers.title: Sorting in PRAM, Parallel Comparison Model and Parallel External Memory Model
papers.abstract: We study the problem of sorting on the Parallel Random Access Machine (PRAM), Parallel Comparison Model (PCM) and Parallel External Memory Model (PEM). On PRAM, we present a Concurrent Read Exclusive Write algorithm that runs in $O(\log n)$ time with $n$ processors; our algorithm is very different from Cole's Merge Sort. On PCM, we present the first optimal algorithm for sorting after AKS; our algorithm runs in $O(\log n/\logα)$ comparison rounds with $nα$ processors, for $1\leqα\leq n$. On PEM, we present a Concurrent Read Exclusive Write algorithm that sorts $N$ elements in $O\left(\log\frac{N}{B}\right)$ I/O rounds with $p\geq \frac{N}{B}$ processors.

papers.title: Unitary $KK$ and $Kπ$ inputs for an amplitude analysis of the $D^+ \to K^-K^+π^+$ decay
papers.abstract: Charge-Parity Violation (CPV) is expected in three-body charm decays. In particular, in the singly Cabibbo suppressed decay process $D^+ \to K^-K^+π^+$; in which an amplitude analysis is required to understand the dynamics of Final State Interactions (FSI) and the mechanism that can generate CPV. In this work, we show the prospects of analysing recent data from the Large Hadron Collider beauty (LHCb) experiment at CERN, with a precise theoretical model expected to reveal CPV mechanisms. Previous analyses of the $D^+ \to K^-K^+π^+$ decay were unable to satisfactorily describe the data using the Isobar Model. Currently, LHCb has a sample of charmed meson decays with around 100 million events for the $D^+ \to K^-K^+π^+$ decay, so a more robust phenomenological model is needed to describe such a large data set. The present model has allowed the inclusion of hadronic FSI and will, in prospect, introduce three-body effects, overcoming some limitations of the Isobar Model, and has all factors necessary to reveal the presence of CPV. To do so, it factorizes the weak vertex separated in leading topologies and relies on extensions of Resonant Chiral Perturbation Theory to describe FSI. As a proof-of-concept, a toy dataset of the S-wave of the most recent amplitude analysis of $D^+ \to K^-K^+π^+$, by the CLEO-c collaboration, was fitted with this model.
