Bond-current density calculations show that transport is confined to the resonant channel with negligible leakage into neighboring outputs, yielding channel selectivity approaching unity for all resonant modes. The architecture is compatible with Si/SiGe and GaAs/AlGaAs platforms and can be extended to more channels, offering a route toward programmable quantum routing and resonant-tunneling-based quantum circuitry.

papers.title: Ensembles of Random Partition-Based Models under Covariate Shift
papers.abstract: Distribution shifts, including covariate shifts, are ubiquitous in real-world applications of machine learning. Empirical evidence suggests that, across a variety of models with and without downstream adaptation, ensembles tend to be more robust to covariate shift than single models. We extend the theory of covariate shift severity from single models to ensembles, providing theoretical justification for the empirical trends. We introduce new discrepancy measures of covariate shift severity to control the risk of partition-based kernel estimators. We then show that with sufficient ensemble size, these models can achieve minimax-optimal risk convergence rates under covariate shift. Our results suggest that modelers can expect to need larger ensemble sizes for more severe covariate shifts.

papers.title: Divisibility Properties of Odd Part and Even Part Sums in Cubic Partitions
papers.abstract: A cubic partition of a positive integer $n$ is a partition of $n$ in which even parts may appear in two distinct colors. The purpose of this paper is to study the arithmetic functions $COS(n)$ and $CES(n)$, which denote the sums of all odd and even parts, respectively, in all cubic partitions of $n$. We obtain their generating functions and divisor-sum formulas, and establish Ramanujan-type congruences modulo $3$, $4$, $5$, and $7$. To prove these congruences, we use Lambert series, classical theta-function identities, dissections, coefficient extraction, and weighted Euler identities.

papers.title: Robust Reconstruction of Power Lines from Incomplete Mobile and Aerial LiDAR Data
papers.abstract: Accurate vegetation-encroachment assessment and risk mitigation require electric utilities to accurately locate and characterize distribution-network assets, including poles and power lines, and distinguish among medium-voltage, low-voltage, neutral, and telecommunication lines. Mobile and aerial Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) point clouds provide detailed 3D representations of these assets and their surroundings. However, power-line detection and reconstruction remain challenging because conductor returns are often sparse, incomplete, noisy, or occluded by vegetation. These challenges are especially significant in distribution networks, where lower pole heights and complex line configurations place conductors close to trees. In addition, mobile and aerial LiDAR datasets differ substantially in point density, viewing geometry, spatial coverage, and occlusion patterns. We propose a robust and automated reconstruction method combining scaled density-based clustering, robust polynomial fitting, and iterative fragment merging to recover individual conductors under severe data incompleteness and occlusion. Following semantic classification, the same reconstruction pipeline processes both mobile and aerial LiDAR data without modality-specific code or parameter tuning. The method is evaluated through degradation experiments, benchmarking, parameter sensitivity analysis, and large-scale validation. On the aerial dataset, it achieves 96.87% precision, 96.66% recall, a 96.76% F$_1$-score, and a geometric RMSE of 0.127 m. On the mobile dataset, where conductor-level reference annotations were unavailable, it achieves a point-to-model RMSE of 0.045 m and a reconstruction coverage of 95.27%. Source code, documentation, and evaluation data are publicly available at https://github.com/varen-project.

papers.title: The P-Ideal Dichotomy and the Failure of Two-Cardinal Square Principles
papers.abstract: We prove that the $\mathrm{P}$-ideal dichotomy implies the negation of the square principle $\square(λ, ω)$ for every regular cardinal $λ\geqω_2$.

papers.title: Response to "Late Time Dynamical Dark Energy and the CMB-Distance Ladder Tension"
papers.abstract: We respond to the recent paper by Efstathiou (arXiv:2607.29562) who makes several statements that appear to be in conflict with our recent paper (Turner & Huterer, arXiv:2606.05358). We stand by our primary result that direct determinations of $H_0$ can be sensitive to the late-time expansion history. We also point out where there is significant agreement between his work and ours.

papers.title: The Galah survey and symbiotic stars. II. Discovery, validation, and intensive follow-up of 44 new systems accreting at the lowest detectable levels
papers.abstract: We report the discovery, validation, and characterization of 44 new symbiotic stars (SySts) accreting at the lowest detectable levels (Lacc =< 3 Lsun). Candidates were initially selected from the Galah survey among non-pulsating M-type red giants exhibiting Halpha excess. Between 2021 and 2025, these targets were subjected to intensive multi-wavelength campaigns, including ground-based, high-resolution Echelle spectroscopy over 544 nights, multi-epoch flickering searches down to 1 mmag, and UV/X-ray observations with the Swift satellite. Our high-resolution spectra allowed for a detailed investigation of Halpha flux and line-profile variability. Crucially, the radial velocities measured for the M-giant components yielded reliable spectroscopic orbits for 22 objects and preliminary orbits for an additional eight, corroborated by binary-induced modulations in ASAS-SN photometry. Measured accretion levels vary by factors of up to 20X, emphasizing the need for high-sensitivity, long-term monitoring. Swift X-ray data exclude neutron star companions in all targets, consistent with predominance of white-dwarf degenerates in known SySts. Combined with the 33 objects from Paper I, this sample of 77 new SySts significantly exceeds the number of previously known, accreting-only Galactic symbiotic stars, constituting the bulk of the low-accretion (LowAcc) variety discovered to date and representing >10 percent of all known SySts in the Galaxy. As SySts likely spend most of their lifetimes in LowAcc faint states, characterizing this population is essential for estimating the total Galactic SySt population and evaluating the role of SySts as Type Ia supernova progenitors or sources of UV excess in elliptical galaxies.

papers.title: Excitation factors and exceptional points of Kerr--Newman quasinormal modes
papers.abstract: We study excitation factors and investigate exceptional points (EPs) of Kerr--Newman quasinormal modes using the exact separated gravitoelectromagnetic equations. At fixed charge, the magnitudes of the excitation factors for the gravitational-led modes studied here decrease with increasing spin, whereas those for electromagnetic-led modes exhibit both monotonic and nonmonotonic behavior. The magnitude of the excitation factor for the first overtone can be comparable to or larger than that for the fundamental mode. We identify 42 EPs at which pairs of modes coalesce in the gravitational-led and electromagnetic-led sectors. Some EPs form sequences involving successive overtone pairs, with higher-overtone pairs coalescing progressively closer to the extremal limit. The additional EPs identified outside these sequences all share the same mode-pair labels as sequence members, but occur at different values of the black hole spin and charge. These findings clarify how rotation and charge shape the relative excitation strengths of different modes and the pattern of mode coalescence in the non-Hermitian spectrum of Kerr--Newman black holes.

papers.title: Empirical Bayes Flow Matching for Continuous Cryo-EM Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: We address the problem of learning generative priors over high-dimensional latent variables from indirect, noisy observations, with a focus on continuous heterogeneity in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). In this setting, 3D atomic structures $x \in \mathbb{R}^{3N_a}$ are never directly observed and must be inferred from 2D projection images $y$ generated by a complex, non-linear forward operator. We propose Empirical Bayes Flow Matching (EB-FM), a method that learns a flow matching prior $p_θ(x)$ directly from observations using a Monte Carlo stochastic approximation Expectation-Maximization framework. EB-FM alternates between an E-step that performs approximate posterior sampling from $p_θ(x \mid y)$ via guided flow-based generation while maintaining persistent latent estimates through stochastic approximation, and an M-step that updates the flow model using these stabilized latent variables as training targets. This approach eliminates the need for pretraining on clean data and naturally accommodates non-linear forward models. We validate our method on controlled inverse problems using two-moons and MNIST data, and demonstrate its effectiveness on simulated cryo-EM data with known poses, showing that EB-FM can recover continuous distributions of protein conformations directly in atomic-coordinate space.

papers.title: Exact association-test distributions for prior-informed stepwise SNP prioritization
papers.abstract: Prioritizing causal variants in Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) is challenging due to linkage disequilibrium and high dimensionality. We propose an iterative algorithm for the selection of genetic variables that allows the integration of biological priors. The proposed algorithm requires the specification of the power function of a test statistic and incorporates a priori information on each SNP. We derive the approximate and exact distributions of several commonly used test statistics. At each step of the proposed algorithm, we select the SNP with the largest a posteriori probability of being causal. We consider several stopping criteria for the algorithm. We conduct comprehensive simulation studies to assess the performance of several versions of the proposed algorithm and to make a comparison to some existing competitors. The use of the proposed prioritization algorithm is illustrated with a cis-eQTL application to a human gene-expression data, using European discovery and Yoruba cross-population replication.

papers.title: Signature of exocomet transits observed with Ariel
papers.abstract: We investigate the potential of the Ariel space telescope to detect and characterise exocomet transits through their wavelength-dependent photometric signatures. Building on a radiative-transfer framework, we model exocomet transits for three representative dust morphologies, three grain-size distributions, and four homogeneous dust compositions using synthetic photometric bands covering the Ariel wavelength range. The modelled events typically last 1-2 days and produce photometric variations of a few millimagnitudes. We find that the wavelength dependence of the transit signal provides stronger diagnostics of the dust properties than transit morphology alone. In particular, colour variations relative to the VISPhot band and their wavelength-dependent slopes separate the considered compositions into two broad groups: carbonaceous dust and graphite, and olivine and pyroxene. While the compositions within each group show similar behaviour, the two groups remain distinguishable across the dust morphologies and grain sizes considered. We further assess the detectability of these signals using the $β$~Pictoris spectral energy distribution and ArielRad simulations. Integrating over broad synthetic photometric bands substantially improves the signal-to-noise ratio, allowing millimagnitude-level signals to be detected with short integration times for sufficiently bright targets. Ariel's simultaneous optical-to-infrared coverage therefore offers the possibility not only of detecting exocomet transits, but also of characterising their chromatic signatures and constraining broad classes of dust properties. We also discuss the limitations of the modelling assumptions and the potential of coordinated observations with long-baseline photometric missions.

papers.title: TAQ-MOTR: Tracking-Aware Detection Query Formation for End-to-End Multiple Object Tracking
papers.abstract: Tracking-by-propagation (TBP) methods perform end-to-end multi-object tracking by propagating track queries across frames, jointly handling detection and identity association without heuristic post-processing while naturally modeling temporal information. However, as detection and association are tightly coupled, detection queries in TBP are expected to discover currently untracked objects and provide complementary current-frame evidence for challenging tracks whose queries and identities are retained. Existing methods largely inherit detection-query formation from single-frame detection and construct such queries before the decoder with little awareness of trajectory states. Consequently, currently untracked objects may be missed, while challenging tracked objects with reduced visibility under occlusion may lack complementary evidence, causing association failures or duplicate responses. To address these issues, we propose TAQ-MOTR, a tracking-aware detection query formation framework that employs a pre-decoder Hybrid Query Generator (HQG) to fuse current-frame image features, track memory, and learnable memory. By conditioning detection queries on trajectory states, TAQ-MOTR adapts them to \rev{the discovery of currently untracked objects and tracked-object complementation We further introduce a training-only auxiliary detection branch whose one-to-one label assignment is decoupled from that of the main tracking branch, providing additional detection supervision to strengthen the shared HQG and decoder for the discovery of currently untracked objects. TAQ-MOTR improves performance on DanceTrack, SportsMOT, and BFT, achieving 72.0 HOTA, 63.1 AssA, and 76.6 IDF1 on the DanceTrack test set. Code is available at https://github.com/Magicmiya/TAQ-MOTR

papers.title: Diffusion Plug-in Priors for Self-Supervised Ultrasound Video Restoration
papers.abstract: Ultrasound videos are limited by hardware-constrained spatial resolution and signal-dependent speckle, while paired low- and high-resolution acquisitions for supervised restoration are rarely available. We aim to jointly super-resolve and despeckle ultrasound videos without paired training data or network retraining. We propose UltraDiff, which uses a frozen pre-trained diffusion model (DM) as a plug-in prior and restores each frame by optimizing the latent seed of the DM sampler under a range-constrained maximum a posteriori formulation. We derive a speckle-aware data-fidelity term from a Rayleigh scale-family model and characterize its relative-residual and variance-adaptive weighting properties. We further introduce a stabilized fidelity that is bounded below and strictly convex in log intensity for positive observations in its unclamped form. A total-variation regularizer complements the DM prior, and a temporal seed update warm-starts each frame from the optimized seed of its predecessor. On EchoNet-LVH videos with simulated speckle and additive noise, UltraDiff with a natural-image prior improves PSNR by 1.24\,dB over the strongest baseline, and ultrasound-related priors improve it further. On real clinical echocardiography videos, UltraDiff reduces the mean absolute error of zero-shot ejection fraction (EF) prediction from 7.31 to 6.37 EF points relative to DUP, the strongest baseline. Combining a speckle-aware fidelity with frozen diffusion priors enables ground-truth-free ultrasound video restoration that benefits downstream measurement. UltraDiff needs neither paired data nor retraining and is not tied to a specific diffusion checkpoint. Code associated with this work will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

papers.title: Multi-Objective Generative Optimization via Expected Hypervolume Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Scientific discovery requires plausible designs spanning useful trade-offs among competing properties: a molecule with strong binding affinity, for example, may be difficult to synthesize. Pretrained generative models, e.g., flow and diffusion generators, provide a foundation for proposing such designs, but steering them toward high-quality, complementary trade-offs remains challenging. Inference-time search incurs high per-sample costs, while fine-tuning typically relies on fixed per-candidate rewards that do not capture how designs complement one another. We introduce Hypervolume Fine-Tuning (HVFT), which adapts a single pretrained generator to maximize the expected hypervolume of its samples while controlling departure from the pretrained distribution. Expected hypervolume jointly rewards candidate quality and collective trade-off coverage. Nonetheless, we show that it cannot be expressed as the expectation of a fixed per-candidate reward and therefore cannot be optimized directly with standard techniques. A key observation of this work is that its first variation corresponds to the expected marginal hypervolume contribution of a candidate, which yields a tractable adaptive reward via an unbiased estimator based on model samples. HVFT uses this reward to decompose the objective into a sequence of KL-proximal scalar-reward subproblems. We establish concavity, relative smoothness, and convergence guarantees for the resulting distributional procedure. Across therapeutic-peptide and molecular design tasks spanning discrete diffusion and continuous flow-matching models, HVFT achieves state-of-the-art expected hypervolume and trade-off coverage.

papers.title: Privacy for Free in Efficient Agnostic Halfspace Learning
papers.abstract: We provide the first computationally efficient, differentially private algorithms for agnostically learning halfspaces. In particular, we study three different settings of agnostic learning: improper learning under Gaussian and log-concave marginals; proper learning under Gaussian marginals; and semi-agnostic learning under Gaussian marginals. In all three aforementioned settings, the added cost in the sample complexity due to privacy matches the respective non-private sample complexity, implying that we get privacy for free.

papers.title: LIBRA: Programmatic Induction of Executable Tool Libraries
papers.abstract: Large language model agents increasingly retrieve tools from large catalogs, yet most retrievers rank each tool independently by request similarity. For multi tool tasks, this recovers the goal matching tool while omitting prerequisite tools required by the workflow. We introduce LIBRA, a framework for Library Induction by Runtime Assembly that turns a flat tool catalog into an executable tool library. An LLM proposes per tool contracts of candidate invocations, reusable outputs and state changes, and success conditions; LIBRA then tests these compositions in a sandbox and retains the relations supported at runtime. Constructed before user queries, the library requires no dependency annotations, tool use trajectories, or task specific training, and supports both one-shot and agentic retrieval. On AppWorld, BFCL, and SciToolEval, LIBRA improves one-shot Recall and NDCG over the same dense retriever by 7.9 and 3.7 percentage points on average. Within ToolReAGt, it yields corresponding gains of 4.5 and 2.9 points after ten retrieval iterations.

papers.title: Relative cohomology and base-change
papers.abstract: In this note we prove a simple generalization of cohomology and base-change which seems to be missing from standard sources. We illustrate its usefulness by providing an alternative proof of a result of Ishimura on descent of vector bundles along blowups at a smooth center.

papers.title: Non-local approximations for the Schrödinger operator with a general point interaction via the non-relativistic limit
papers.abstract: We consider the one-dimensional Dirac operator $D_{A,c}$ with a general, not necessarily self-adjoint, point interaction at the origin, whose strength is described by an arbitrary complex $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ and suitably rescaled by the speed of light $c$, together with its non-local approximations $D_{A,c}^ε$ obtained by replacing the Dirac distribution by a rank-one projection onto a scaled function $v_ε$. It is known that $D_{A,c}^ε\to D_{A,c}$ as $ε\to 0+$ and that $D_{A,c}-c^2/2$ converges, as $c\to+\infty$, to the Schrödinger operator $H_A$ with the general point interaction, both in the norm resolvent sense. We prove that the first convergence is uniform with respect to $c$ in a neighbourhood of $+\infty$, and we provide explicit rates of convergence. Combining this with an explicit computation of the non-relativistic limit of $D_{A,c}^ε$ for fixed $ε$, we show that the two limits can be interchanged and that the corresponding double limit exists. As a by-product we obtain a family of non-local, rank-two approximations $H_A^ε$ of $H_A$ that converge to $H_A$ in the norm resolvent sense. Contrary to the relativistic setting, the coupling constants of $H_A^ε$ are renormalized; we give an explicit formula for this renormalization.

papers.title: Physics-informed traditional and generative Mori-Zwanzig-reduced models for multiscale systems
papers.abstract: Model reduction via the Mori-Zwanzig (MZ) formalism is well understood for coarse-grained representations constructed from standard basis functions such as Fourier functions. We show that the same formalism can be used to build reduced-order models in bases discovered by physics-informed machine learning. The fluctuation-dissipation theorem (FDT) is used to close the resulting non-Markovian evolution equations for the expansion coefficients of the learned basis. We further introduce a complementary, generative closure model. Relative to the Markovian dynamics alone, both the MZ and generative closures substantially improve predictions of the filtered states.

papers.title: 2D Navier-Stokes with viscosity-dependent Navier slip: strong convergence for unbounded initial velocity
papers.abstract: For the two-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with Navier friction on a smooth, bounded, simply connected domain, we establish strong vorticity convergence along a subsequence in the vanishing viscosity limit for initial vorticity in $L^p$ with $p>1$. The friction coefficients may grow as viscosity vanishes under an explicit growth restriction depending on $p$, which includes regimes of vanishing slip length. The main challenge, even for viscosity-independent friction, is to control the vorticity generated at the boundary. We split the vorticity into contributions from the initial data and the boundary. By combining renormalization and estimates for the normal velocity near the boundary, we show that the boundary contribution vanishes in the inviscid limit. As a consequence, the limiting Euler solutions conserve kinetic energy.

papers.title: The Hidden Markov Ising Model with Exogenous Covariates
papers.abstract: The Ising model, a type of Markov Random Field, from statistical physics has a long history of modeling spatial and network data as well as particle interactions. In this work, we consider inserting the Ising model into the framework of a Hidden Markov Model, a type of Bayesian Network, to model temporal state changes in a sequence of Ising observations. While this is entirely a discrete probability model, a main challenge is the fitting of such a probabilistic graphical model due to the exponential intractability of normalizing constants within the Ising model. To circumvent this problem, we consider the usage of maximum pseudolikelihood estimators that have a long history in Markov Random Fields. Validity of the pseudolikelihood Baum-Welch algorithm, model identifiability under likelihood, and consistency for large networks is also proved. The proposed Hidden Markov Ising Model is further extended to incorporate exogenous variables resulting in a hybrid hidden Markov autologistic model with graphical dependencies integrated into the model. This model is applied to a five year sequence of weekly gun violence events across the 3109 counties of the continental United States to identify state changes in gun violence activity from 2021 to 2025.

papers.title: H-sober spaces and Hofmann-Mislove type theorems
papers.abstract: A $T_0$-space is called $ω$-sober if every irreducible closed subset having a countable dense subset is the closure of a unique point. This is precisely $H$-sobriety for the countable irreducible subset system $\mathcal R^ω$. We give two natural Hofmann--Mislove representations in the general $H$-sobriety framework: filters induced by $H$-sets of $X$ characterize $H$-sobriety, whereas filters induced by $H$-sets of the Smyth power space characterize super $H$-sobriety. Their relation is expressed by property $Q$. A minimal closed set argument with a countable selection proves that $\mathcal R^ω$ has property $Q$. Consequently, $X$ is $ω$-sober if and only if its Smyth power space is $ω$-sober, equivalently, every countable irreducible compact-family filter has a compact saturated representation. We also obtain equivalent recovery, compact-intersection and representation conditions for an enlarged class containing the proper Scott-open filters with countable open bases and the filters induced by countable irreducible subsets. A further equivalent formulation uses traces on countable subspaces. The filtered-family specializations recover well-filteredness and $ω$-well-filteredness. Explicit examples show that $ω$-sobriety strictly implies $ω$-well-filteredness, which strictly implies representation for countable open bases alone.

papers.title: Parallel Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics in Python: Task- and Data-Parallel SINDy with Numba, OpenMP, Threads and Multiprocessing for the Lorenz and Rössler Systems
papers.abstract: The sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics (SINDy) recovers interpretable governing equations from time-series data by sparse regression over a library of candidate functions. As data sets, candidate libraries and the number of repeated fits grow, the cost of SINDy becomes dominated by the evaluation of the library matrix and its least-squares problems. We present an open-source Python implementation of SINDy in which a single set of loop-based kernels is just-in-time compiled with Numba and executed on a shared-memory multicore node by four interchangeable back ends: Numba prange, OpenMP directives through PyOMP, Python threads that release the global interpreter lock, and multiprocessing with shared memory. The normal equations are accumulated in one cache-blocked pass over the data, with an automatic fallback to a tall-skinny QR reduction for ill-conditioned problems. Two decompositions are studied on the Lorenz and Rössler systems: an ensemble (task-parallel) workload of 960 independent identifications and a library (data-parallel) workload of one trajectory with $2\times10^7$ samples and a fifth-order library of 56 candidate terms. All back ends recover the exact sparsity pattern in every identification, with coefficient errors identical to PySINDy. On a dual-socket Intel Xeon E5-2650 v4 node of the University of Houston-Downtown HPC cluster (24 cores, 48 hardware threads), the compiled serial code is 4.3-5.6x faster than PySINDy, the parallel back ends reach speed-ups of 14.8-20.3 on 24 cores (parallel efficiency 0.61-0.84), and the overall time to solution is reduced by up to 117x with respect to PySINDy. We analyse the differences between the back ends, the effect of the two sockets and of hyper-threading, and give practical recommendations.

papers.title: Boundary Projection Acceleration for 2D One-cell Inversions in the Scattering Limit
papers.abstract: Efficient radiation transport on modern high-performance computers requires algorithms that expose spatial parallelism while maintaining robust convergence. One-cell inversion (OCI) replaces the spatially sequential transport sweep of source iteration with a cell-local solve, making discrete ordinates transport space-parallel, but its spectral radius approaches unity in diffusive problems, and existing accelerators such as transport synthetic acceleration reintroduce sweeps. Here we show that projecting the OCI residual onto a low-order angular space on cell boundaries accelerates convergence in scattering-dominated problems without a transport sweep. We implement the projection in a two-dimensional simple-corner-balance discretization with two angular bases: a linear ($P_1$) basis and one augmented with a quadrant moment ($P_1Q$). Fourier analysis of an infinite homogeneous medium shows that both corrections reduce the spectral radius in optically thick, highly scattering regimes, with $P_{1}Q$ being most effective. Across several test problems, including a modified version of the void-duct streaming benchmark, the method accelerates diffusive and scattering cases but does not uniformly improve convergence in streaming dominated problems. We also find that $P_{1}Q$ is a more robust accelerator than $P_1$ in situations where the flux has strong angular variation. Boundary projection substantially improves OCI convergence in diffusive regimes, and these results delimit the regimes that require additional stabilization or richer projection spaces.

papers.title: Two examples in amplituhedron tilings
papers.abstract: We give an example of a tiling of the $m=4$ amplituhedron that has fewer cells than that of the magic number conjecture. The tiling uses an injective degree two cell.

papers.title: On the $abc$ conjecture
papers.abstract: Using adelic intersection theory and following the method envisioned by Parshin and Moret-Bailly, we prove a conjecture of Vojta for curves of genus two and a weak form of the $abc$ conjecture

papers.title: Beyond Anonymous Order Flow: Wallet Identity as a Feature for Short-Horizon Return Prediction
papers.abstract: Conventional public order-book data summarize trading without identifying the accounts behind it. Hyperliquid's Level-4 record also exposes persistent pseudonymous wallet addresses. We reconstruct full-depth books from consensus-ordered messages and evaluate wallet identity as a feature for short-horizon return prediction. The July 1-27, 2026 record covers 17.1 billion messages, 14.3 million aggressive orders by 147,113 wallets, and $84.3 billion in taker notional across ten markets. In the three model markets, notional-weighted ten-second markout rankings persist across adjacent ten-day windows (Spearman rho = 0.52); covariate-adjusted validation markouts reach 3.11 basis points in the top ventile. On a 100-millisecond grid, eleven features describing previously scored top-decile wallets raise one-second out-of-sample R2 from 10.88% to 12.

papers.title: Full-Stokes response to a stochastic gravitational-wave background in pulsar timing arrays: Fully analytic overlap reduction functions at finite distance and coherence of close pulsar pairs
papers.abstract: We derive fully analytic overlap reduction functions for the full-Stokes response of a pulsar timing array to an anisotropic tensor gravitational-wave background in general relativity. The response retains both pulsar distances and their complete propagation phases. At each fixed finite sky multipole, the intensity and circular polarization responses reduce to finite combinations involving exponential integrals and logarithms, while the electric and magnetic linear polarization responses require only elementary functions. We evaluate all components through $\ell=8$. Symmetry separates exact nulls from additional Earth-term nulls that propagation can lift. Even an unpolarized background can produce an imaginary cross-spectrum. For a pair with three-dimensional separation $d$, the pulsar terms can remain coherent when $2πfd/c\lesssim1$, even if both pulsars are many wavelengths from Earth. A uniform approximation retaining all four Earth and pulsar terms connects this regime to the short-wavelength limit, and a rotationally invariant relation fixes the leading transverse magnetic response. Common-distance errors cancel from the aligned pair phase, while relative-depth errors directly affect coherence. Under Gaussian differential averaging, fixed low-multipole norms and the squared norm summed over all multipoles decay at different rates as the response shifts to higher multipoles. Published pulsar configurations illustrate the roles of distance accuracy, bandwidth, and timing fits. At fixed pointwise intensity, a polarization covariance bound and a relative-depth noise budget quantify when differencing suppresses the background. Independent sky integration and matched-accuracy benchmarks test the analytic expressions over the parameter ranges studied.

papers.title: Fusing Earth observation embeddings and spaceborne terrain with meteorological forcing for flood peak depth prediction from high-water marks
papers.abstract: Flood peak depth on normally dry land governs damage and risk to life, but is observed only sparsely, by post-event high-water mark (HWM) surveys, and depth derived from satellite flood extent is produced after the event and inherits the vertical error of the digital elevation model (DEM) it is computed from. Deep-learning flood models have in turn been trained on hydrodynamic simulations rather than on observed depths. We ask whether flood peak depth can be learned from field observations and predicted before the peak from spaceborne terrain, geospatial foundation-model embeddings and antecedent meteorological forcing. We assembled 5689 USGS HWM surveys from 39 events (2011-2025) in 24 U.S. states and Puerto Rico, assigned each a peak time from nearby sensors, paired each with a rain-free window at the same site, and linked them to Copernicus GLO-30 terrain, AlphaEarth embeddings and 144 h of hourly forcing masked to the lead time. A cross-modal fusion network trained on these observations predicts depth at the surveyed marks with a mean absolute error of 0.39 m 6 h ahead of the peak. Supervision by surveyed depth corrects the DEM error implicitly: differencing the measured peak water level with the same DEM gives 0.93 m at the same marks, 2.4 times larger, although it uses the measured water level and the model does not. Forcing accounts for 77% of the attributed reduction in depth error; terrain and the embeddings are statistically equivalent to each other and contribute the remaining 23%. On eleven held-out events the model still separates flooded from rain-free conditions but no longer resolves depth at the marks (R2 = 0.03), so the skill reported here is confined to the events and regions sampled. Field-surveyed depths can thus supervise flood depth prediction and correct terrain error that extent-based estimation cannot, while transfer to unseen storms remains the open problem.

papers.title: Efficient Equilibrium Computation in Colonel Blotto Games
papers.abstract: Colonel Blotto is a fundamental resource-allocation game in which two players divide their budgets across battlefields, and the higher allocation on each battlefield wins its value. The problem of computing an equilibrium efficiently has remained unresolved for its classical continuous version with arbitrary budgets and with values that may vary across battlefields but are the same for both players. We give a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme that computes an $\varepsilon$-Nash equilibrium in time polynomial in the input length and $1/\varepsilon$, and nearly linear in the input length for fixed $\varepsilon$. For sufficiently balanced budgets and battlefield values, we also compute exact equilibria in linear time.

papers.title: Fairness Metrics based on the AUC in Clinical Predictive AI
papers.abstract: Fairness evaluation of clinical prediction models for binary outcomes often involves fairness metrics that compare the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC, or c-statistic) across subgroups. However, the AUC has been shown to be a non-collapsible metric, meaning that its subgroup specific and overall values are not directly comparable as often implicitly assumed. This raises important questions about how existing AUC-based fairness metrics should be used and interpreted. We examine eight AUC-based fairness metrics proposed in the literature, including: within-group AUC parity; cross-group AUC (xAUC) parity; gap-to-overall AUC; equity-scaled AUC; minimum-based metrics; $\mathrm{xAUC}^1$; $\mathrm{xAUC}^0$; and $\mathrm{xAUC}^1$ or $\mathrm{xAUC}^0$ parity. We characterise their estimands, relate them to the decomposition of overall AUC (into within- and cross-group components), and critically appraise them. We then illustrate their behaviour using simulations based on the EuroSCORE II, a clinical prediction model for in-hospital mortality. We recommend reporting an AUC matrix, containing the overall AUC and all within- and cross-group AUC components, alongside population characteristics. When fairness metrics are needed, we recommend reporting the within-group AUC parity, with cross-group AUC parity providing supplementary information but requiring caution due to its potential conflict with calibration. Metrics involving $\mathrm{xAUC}^1$ and $\mathrm{xAUC}^0$ have merit, summarising within- and cross-group AUCs into single values, but their interpretation is non-trivial, and they should be used with caution. Gap-to-overall AUC, equity-scaled AUC, and minimum-based metrics compare quantities that should not be compared and it is unclear how to operationalise them, making them not fit for purpose and generally not recommended.

papers.title: PLANTEUR: A Crop-Type Segmentation Benchmark for Tropical Regions
papers.abstract: We introduce PLANTEUR, a benchmark for crop-type mapping from satellite images in the French overseas territories. Building on the PASTIS design, PLANTEUR provides georeferenced and aligned Sentinel-2, Sentinel-1, and Landsat-8 sequences with parcel-derived labels spanning six tropical regions and an 8-class label space. We define both a standard test split and a leave-one-island-out protocol to measure cross-territory generalization, and evaluate fully supervised models, linear probes, and fine-tuned foundation models. The benchmark code and data are open source and available on GitHub and Hugging Face.

papers.title: Learning curves in natural and artificial systems
papers.abstract: A general mathematical model of experience formation is considered, in which the learning level is defined as the probability that the next value of the uncertainty factor has already been mastered and not forgotten. Within this model the shape of the learning curve is derived, and it turns out to be determined primarily by the distribution of situation occurrence: a uniform distribution yields an exponential curve, whereas a power-law distribution yields a power-law curve whose exponent equals the ratio of the distribution exponent to that same exponent increased by one. Both mechanisms generating power-law curves, established earlier in the analysis of debugging, assembly and repair activities, are shown to have been independently rediscovered in deep learning theory as the "frequency" and "spectral" mechanisms of scaling laws for artificial neural networks, while the exponential curves of machine learning (contraction operators, strongly convex optimization, stationary reinforcement) are generated by the same constancy of the contraction coefficient that was revealed half a century earlier in models of radioactive decay, the first-order lag element, and others. A solution is given for the problem of choosing a training distribution that differs from the deployment distribution. A methodological consequence is discussed: three distinct mechanisms generate curves indistinguishable in shape, so an observed learning curve does not allow one to judge the "internal" structure of the learning system.

papers.title: Post-Inference Model Chaining: A Problem Statement and a Model-based Bootstrap for Training End-to-End Digital Twins
papers.abstract: End-to-end digital twins can be constructed by fitting separate stage models and connecting them after inference. We investigate the Frequentist prediction properties of a commonly used Monte Carlo simulation scheme that forwards complete predictive draws through such a chain when measured stage outputs contain independent normal errors, but the latent stage means are deterministic. Analytical two-stage examples show persistent asymptotic interval and coverage inflation and, with quadratic propagation, mean bias dependent on the parameters to be estimated. Simulations of four- and eight-stage linear-quadratic univariate chains with 7, 15 or 30 training runs demonstrate pronounced input-dependent distortions. A diagnostic using error-free latent training predictors shows that the effect is mainly not attributable to errors in variables, but to the MCSim approach even showing underestimation of coverage. We propose a model-based bootstrap: an initial chain forwards fitted means, bootstrap chains are refitted on fixed-center bootstrap data while forwarding their mean prediction, and a target-stage future error enters a studentized prediction root. Across the investigated scenarios, relative mean bias is substantially reduced, and coverage is closer to the nominal 90%. At sample size 30, the eight-stage bootstrap has mean width ratios of 1.16-1.42 relative to the known-parameter normal reference, compared with 4.11-4.97 for observed-to-observed MCSim. These results support improved endpoint prediction in the tested setting. Further investigations of the bootstrap scheme in the supplement for a bivariate 6-stage process show similar satisfactory results.

papers.title: CQ-collocation BEMs for exterior wave propagation problems: the 3D Neumann case
papers.abstract: In this paper, we consider three-dimensional exterior wave propagation problems with non-homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions. We reformulate the problem as a space-time boundary integral equation involving a hypersingular operator. To solve the resulting formulation, we combine Lubich's convolution quadrature with a shifted collocation boundary element discretization and investigate numerically the efficiency, stability, and convergence of the resulting numerical scheme. Numerical tests show that the proposed approach achieves an accuracy comparable to that of Lubich's convolution quadrature combined with a Galerkin boundary element method, and provide numerical evidence of the unconditional stability of the collocation scheme.

papers.title: Regret-based Characterization, Information Limits, and the Sample Complexity of Auditing Adaptive Policies
papers.abstract: A policy can earn its performance by where it locates on average or by reacting to information. For any Markov policy $π$ in a finite-horizon MDP, let $ν$ be its open-loop marginal, which plays $π$'s average action distribution at each step. We show that $J(π)-J(ν)$ equals $\sum_t tr Cov(Q^ν_t,π_t)$ under endogenous dynamics. Audits based on immediate costs alone can have the wrong sign. Writing the covariance as a joint-versus-product gap gives the bound $|J(π)-J(ν)|\le\sum_t span_t\sqrt{I(s_t;a_t)/2}$, with a sharp constant. Hence, an MDP's adaptivity gap is bounded by the information that its optimal policy uses. Estimating $J(π)-J(ν)$ from $π$'s own bandit-feedback logs takes $Θ(\barχ^2 \log(1/η)/δ^2)$ rounds, where $\barχ^2$ is an average $χ^2$-divergence. At the same time, deterministic non-constant policies cannot be audited at all. We also provide an importance-sampling auditor for episodic MDPs.

papers.title: Beyond the Bochner Method: Optimal Spectral Gaps for Block Dynamics of Spin Systems like the $O(N)$ Model
papers.abstract: Let $μ$ be a probability distribution on a spin system with $n$ sites and possibly infinite spin spaces. We prove local-to-global spectral-gap bounds for block Glauber dynamics. Given a symmetric, entrywise nonnegative matrix $A$ with zero diagonal and $λ_{\max}(A)<1$ encoding local spectral bounds for a spin system, we derive global spectral-gap bounds for block dynamics on its marginal distributions. These bounds are sharp: the Gaussian system with covariance $(I-A)^{-1}$ attains equality for every choice of disjoint blocks. Our proof extends the Bochner method through an abstract inequality for orthogonal projections on Hilbert spaces. As an application, we prove that Glauber dynamics for the $O(N)$ model, with $N\geq 2$, arbitrary external fields, and couplings of either sign, has spectral gap at least $(1-\|J_{\mathrm{abs}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}/N)/n$, where $J$ is the interaction matrix and $J_{\mathrm{abs}}=(|J_{ij}|)$. We also obtain spectral bounds for swap walks and local spectral expansion of partite simplicial complexes. For complexes formed from disjoint groups of ranks in random flags of subspaces over $\mathbb F_q$, we obtain a one-sided local spectral expansion bound of $2\sqrt q/(q+1)$. This bound is independent of the number and sizes of each group, and is nontrivial for every prime power $q$. Finally, for random forests $F$ of any finite graph with arbitrary positive edge weights, we prove that \[ \Pr(e,f\in F)\le \frac{4}{3} \Pr(e\in F)\Pr(f\in F) \] for distinct edges $e,f$, improving the factor 2 supplied by general log-concavity bounds for matroid independent sets. The argument combines our extended Bochner method with the analysis of an auxiliary real stable polynomial.

papers.title: Santa Claus and Weighted Nash Social Welfare with Subadditive Valuations
papers.abstract: We study max-min allocation (the Santa Claus problem) and weighted Nash social welfare for $n$ agents with subadditive valuations over $m$ indivisible items. Using demand queries, we give randomized polynomial-time approximation algorithms with factors $O(\sqrt n)$ and $O(Γ(w))$, respectively, where $Γ(w)=\exp((\ln n-H(w))/2)$ and $H(w)=-\sum_i w_i\ln w_i$ for positive weights summing to one. Both ratios are independent of $m$. The max-min result improves the $2n-1$ bound of Khot and Ponnuswami (2007). We also give simpler $O(\sqrt n)$ algorithms for additive valuations and for submodular valuations with value queries, improving the $O(\sqrt{n\log n})$ bound of Saha and Srinivasan (2018) in the additive case. For Nash welfare, $Γ(w)=1$ for equal weights and $Γ(w)\le\sqrt n$ in general. We prove a configuration-LP integrality gap of $Θ(Γ(w))$ for every prescribed weight vector, even for XOS valuations. For every fixed $D>0$, we also prove information-theoretic approximation lower bounds of $Ω_D(\sqrt{n/\ln n})$ and $Ω_D(Γ(w)/\sqrt{\ln n})$, respectively, for randomized algorithms making at most $n^D$ adaptive queries. These hold on XOS instances with $m=Θ(n)$ items, even with simultaneous access to value, demand, and XOS supporting-clause oracles. They apply both to guarantees with success probability at least $2/3$ and to guarantees in expected welfare. The weighted bound holds for every prescribed weight vector and is vacuous below one. Thus the oracle lower bounds are within an $O(\sqrt{\ln n})$ factor of our upper bounds, while the configuration-LP gaps match them up to constants. Our algorithms build on random matchings for large items and charge the aggregate loss across configurations to the at most $n$ matched items.

papers.title: Handling Customer Preferences in Last-Mile Location-Routing: A Bilevel Optimization Approach
papers.abstract: This paper introduces the Location-Routing Problem with Delivery Preferences, a last-mile delivery problem with service flexibility that integrates collection-point activation and routing decisions while accounting for customer choice. The company determines which collection points to activate, which customers to offer home delivery, and the corresponding delivery route. Customers subsequently decide whether to accept the proposed home-delivery service or collect their parcels from an activated collection point according to ranked preferences over delivery time intervals and collection points. This hierarchical interaction is modeled through a bilevel optimization framework, which can be formulated as a mixed-integer bilevel program that incorporates compensation mechanisms for service inconvenience. Two equivalent single-level reformulations that exploit the structure of the customers' problems are developed. In addition, a two-phase heuristic is proposed to generate feasible solutions that can be used as warm starts for the formulations. The computational experiments run to compare the performance of the formulations, show that the warm-start strategy becomes particularly effective as the instance size increases. The comparison with a benchmark model that ignores customer preferences indicates that explicitly accounting for customer choice alters the resulting location-routing configuration while improving customer preference satisfaction at a small increase in the company's overall cost. These findings highlight the importance of jointly considering operational efficiency, service flexibility, and customer autonomy in last-mile delivery planning.

papers.title: Diagnosis by Composition: Detecting and Localizing Unseen Diseases by Composing Learned Radiological Findings
papers.abstract: Deep models for radiological diagnosis are typically trained to predict disease labels directly from images, which limits them to diseases seen during training and makes their decisions hard to interpret in radiologists' terms. Radiology, however, proceeds from visual findings to disease through published guidelines that make this decision rule explicit, interpretable, and reproducible. We introduce diagnosis by composition (DbC), a representation learning framework that encodes this findings-first logic. DbC learns a vocabulary of radiological findings by aligning image features with the text embeddings of the findings, each finding represented as a dense map over the scan. A disease is defined by a set of required findings derived from its guidelines, and its diagnosis map is a fixed, parameter-free composition of the corresponding finding maps. Because the finding-to-disease mapping is derived from guidelines rather than learned, DbC is interpretable and auditable by design, can extend to new diseases by specifying their findings without retraining, and can diagnose unseen diseases by composing their findings. On multi-phase liver CT, DbC detects and localizes unseen diseases, rare diseases from a different institution, and an external cohort significantly better than all comparators, including models that align images with disease names. DbC also improves detection and localization in the fully supervised setting and remains superior across training-set sizes. Although demonstrated on liver CT, DbC applies wherever radiological guidelines define diseases through findings.

papers.title: Scalable Bayesian inference for time-discretised Markov jump processes via exchangeable particle Gibbs
papers.abstract: Inference in stochastic reaction-network models, such as the susceptible-exposed-infectious-recovered (SEIR) epidemic model, is crucial for understanding the dynamics of interacting systems in epidemiology, ecology, and systems biology. These models are typically represented as Markov jump processes (MJPs), with discrete, noisy observations and intractable likelihoods. Particle Markov chain Monte Carlo (PMCMC) offers a natural mechanism for inference on these hidden Markov models, but, even in moderate dimensional state spaces, particle degeneracy typically leads to poor mixing of the PMCMC algorithm. This paper focuses on improving the efficiency of particle Gibbs for inference on reaction networks by addressing the degeneracy problem. Building on recent work on the exchangeable particle Gibbs (xPG) sampler for diffusions, this paper develops a novel version of xPG tailored to discrete-state-space reaction networks, where randomness is driven by Poisson processes rather than Brownian motion. We focus on the $τ$-leap discretisation of the MJPs. The proposed method retains the exchangeability framework of xPG while adapting it to the structural and computational challenges specific to reaction networks. The new method is applied to several examples, including four coupled SEIR models, where it substantially improves mixing efficiency compared with standard particle Gibbs. In this example, xPG improves sample efficiency by more than an order of magnitude relative to standard particle Gibbs, making inference feasible in hours rather than weeks. As part of our tuning strategy, we provide a mechanism for tuning the number of particles that is applicable more generally, to any particle Gibbs algorithm.

papers.title: DynaMite: Dynamic Measurement Scheduling To Accelerate Fault-Tolerant Quantum Programs
papers.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computers run millions of logical cycles to perform quantum error correction (QEC). As logical operations span entire logical cycles, the logical cycle time (LCT) dictates program runtime. Qubit measurements, critical to extract parity information for QEC, are the slowest operations and account for 43-86% of LCT. Measurement latencies impact fidelity: fast measurements lower our ability to correctly classify quantum states, whereas slow measurements increase the likelihood of decoherence. Hardware providers thus calibrate measurement latencies that maximize readout fidelity per qubit and use them to schedule all measurements during program execution. However, calibrated latencies are sub-optimal for logical performance because logical cycles span multiple QEC rounds, during which data qubits are not measured. This increases LCT and logical error rates (LERs) due to decoherence at the logical level. We propose DynaMite, a lightweight real-time measurement latency selection policy built on two key insights. First, logical cycles must use a measurement latency that is fast enough to reduce both LCT and LER for the QEC code, instead of the calibrated latency that only maximizes readout fidelity. Second, not all logical cycles are equal; many do not fully utilize the error budget of the QEC code, i.e., the number of failed parity checks it can tolerate without compromising LER. These cycles could use even faster measurements but do not, because latencies are chosen statically, whereas error information is only available at runtime. DynaMite exploits the fact that a logical cycle comprises multiple QEC rounds and selects the fastest latency for an upcoming round based on the error budget left and rounds remaining. Our evaluations show that DynaMite reduces LCT by 1.69x on average and up to 2.29x, and reduces LER to 0.46x on average and up to 0.13x of baseline.

papers.title: ARLoop: Fully-Open Pre-trained Looped Transformers with Attention Residuals
papers.abstract: Looped transformers increase effective depth by repeatedly applying a shared set of transformer layers, offering a parameter-efficient way to scale computation. However, standard residual connections aggregate information across recurrent depth into a single stream, providing limited control over which intermediate representations from preceding layers should be reused. In this paper, we introduce ARLoop, a looped transformer architecture based on attention residuals, where the input of each layer is selectively aggregated through attention over model depth. Distinct from standard transformers, we find that looped transformers do not require access to the full residual history: sliding-window depth attention matches or outperforms full-history attention at larger recurrent depths. Across controlled experiments with multiple parameter scales (140M and 370M) and recurrent depths (R = 1 to 5), ARLoop consistently outperforms prior residual designs for looped transformers. More importantly, we further scale ARLoop to 0.6B and 1.2B parameters under a realistic LLM pretraining recipe, demonstrating that the gains transfer to realistic pretraining, with particularly strong improvements on math and coding tasks. Our 1.2B model, pretrained on only 0.5T tokens with three recurrences, outperforms Huginn-3.5B (the only fully-open looped LLM as of our release date) across all evaluated tasks and is competitive with similar-sized non-looped models such as Qwen3.5-2B despite being trained on substantially less data.

papers.title: Catalan Hashing: Efficient Linear Probing for Variable-Length Items
papers.abstract: A defining feature of the linear-probing hash table is its spatial locality: at load factor $1 - \varepsilon$, the hash table can be implemented so that each operation scans a single contiguous region of expected size $O(1/\varepsilon)$ (this is known as the \emph{scan cost}). This guarantee, however, relies on all items having unit size. In this paper, we ask whether it is possible to achieve a similar guarantee, but in a hash table that stores items of arbitrary lengths $|x| \ge 1$. The main result of the paper is a new hash table called \emph{Catalan hashing}, which supports amortized expected scan cost $O(|x|/\varepsilon)$ for positive queries, $O(1/\varepsilon)$ for negative queries, and $O(|x|\varepsilon^{-1}\log^{1+δ}|x|)$ for insertions/deletions, for any constant $δ> 0$. As a corollary, we obtain the same bounds in the cache-oblivious model, with a scan cost of $S$ translating to $1 + O(S/B)$ I/Os. Along the way, we introduce several high-level techniques that may be of independent interest; this includes a novel way of using erasure codes in order to perform write optimization within a hash table, and a connection to scheduling that allows us to place elements in a way which avoids clustering at high load factors.

papers.title: The Landau equation: Well-posedness and singularities of homoenergetic solutions
papers.abstract: We consider the inhomogeneous Landau equation and focus on solutions whose density and temperature evolve in time but remain spatially homogeneous. Such solutions are called homoenergetic. We identify one class of initial data for which homoenergetic solutions exist globally in time, and another class for which they develop finite-time hydrodynamic singularities. The initial data are spatially inhomogeneous, neither close to vacuum nor close to equilibrium; both the well-posedness and the finite-time blow-up results hold for all soft and hard potentials.

papers.title: Modulational stability of finite-depth Stokes waves with constant vorticity
papers.abstract: We investigate the effect of constant vorticity on the modulational spectral stability of small-amplitude periodic gravity waves for the two-dimensional finite-depth water-wave system. We derive an explicit stability criterion that agrees with the prediction obtained by Thomas, Kharif and Manna [43] through a nonlinear Schrödinger approximation. For waves propagating to the right, we identify a sharp range of dimensionless positive (counterclockwise) vorticity, for which modulational instability is suppressed at every depth, while at any fixed depth sufficiently strong negative (clockwise) vorticity also restores modulational stability. We give a complete description of the spectrum near the origin and identify a figure-eight spectral curve in the unstable regime. A key distinction from the irrotational case is that the usual Hamiltonian factorization of the linearized operator fails at zero Floquet exponent on the full periodic Sobolev space. We therefore carry out a spectral reduction based on reversibility, without relying on Hamiltonian factorization.

papers.title: Post-stratified importance sampling
papers.abstract: Importance sampling is a building block of modern statistical computing, but the weighted estimate is prone to high or infinite variance. Moreover, its empirical standard error is often unreliable, leaving importance sampling without practical uncertainty quantification. Motivated by multilevel regression and poststratification (MRP) in survey sampling, we propose post-stratified importance sampling (PIS) for estimating target expectations from proposal draws. PIS reformulates arbitrarily high-dimensional weighting into two one-dimensional probabilistic modeling problems: regression for the conditional mean given the importance ratio and marginal density estimation for the importance ratio. Different modeling choices yield a family of PIS estimators, encompassing ordinary importance sampling as a special case. We develop a model-based implementation that combines one-dimensional Gaussian process regression for the conditional mean and score-informed heavy-tailed density estimation for the marginal law, using both the observed weights and the available density evaluations. We study the oracle gains of PIS and establish consistency under general and model-specific conditions. Simulations and applications to cross-validation demonstrate improvements in estimation accuracy and uncertainty quantification.

papers.title: Elliptic and triangular flow responses in O+O and Ne+Ne collisions from hydrodynamics and kinetic theory
papers.abstract: Recent light-ion collisions at the Large Hadron Collider provide an opportunity to investigate the system-size dependence of hydrodynamization and whether the structure of light nuclei can be extracted from collective flow data. Both objectives require an accurate understanding of how the collision dynamics converts initial-state geometry into final-state momentum anisotropies. To this end, and to assess the impact of the experimental results, we compare simulations of O+O and Ne+Ne collisions in hydrodynamic and kinetic theory simulations across opacities. In both ultracentral and peripheral collisions, Ne+Ne-to-O+O elliptic flow ratios are robust against changes in dynamical description, supporting interpretations of data based on nuclear-geometry-driven effects. Triangular-flow ratios instead show substantially stronger sensitivity to nonequilibrium dynamics.

papers.title: Dirac stars in Einstein-Euler-Heisenberg theory
papers.abstract: We study self-gravitating configurations of a charged classical spinor field coupled to gravity and to Euler-Heisenberg (EH) nonlinear electrodynamics, truncated at quartic order. The spinor is gauged under a U(1) field and may carry a quartic self-interaction. For static and spherically symmetric configurations we derive the field equations, reduce them to a dimensionless eigenvalue problem for the spinor frequency and solve it numerically. In the uncharged limit our solutions coincide with the known Dirac stars of general relativity. The electric charge increases the frequency, the mass and the size of the stars, and the maximal mass grows from $0.709$ to $1.027$ (in units of $M_{\rm Pl}^2/μ$) when the charge coupling rises from zero to $0.75$. The quartic term changes the relation between the electric field and the enclosed charge, so that the field inside the star is weaker than in the Maxwell case. Our central result concerns stars with the same number of fermions, and therefore the same total charge. For them the quartic term changes the mass by less than $0.2\%$, but it makes the stars more compact and more strongly bound and shifts the turning point of the family to a smaller particle number. This shift is what lowers the maximal mass, by $9\%$ (from $0.924$ to $0.840$) at charge coupling $0.6$ as the dimensionless EH coupling goes from zero to $200$. In the weak-field regime of quantum electrodynamics (QED) the relative mass correction is $-1.5\times10^{-5}(E_{\max}/E_c)^2$, so the larger couplings describe the quartic model as an effective nonlinear electrodynamics rather than a controlled QED correction. All solutions satisfy the null, weak, strong and dominant energy conditions, show a positive pressure anisotropy, and remain free of horizons. Their stability is discussed through the binding energy and the turning point of the mass curve.

papers.title: Shrinkage prior for implicit generative models
papers.abstract: Implicit generative models based on deep neural networks have revolutionized many scientific fields, from weather research to language generation. They successfully model complex random objects arising in real-world problems. In this work, we propose a sample-efficient training mechanism for these models. Our approach leverages regularized inference with shrinkage priors and generalized Bayes. In the large $p$ (parameter dimension) and small $n$ (sample size) setting, sparsity-inducing priors have been successfully used for linear regression when $p \gg n$. However, their application to implicit generative models remains challenging due to the intractability of the likelihood function. To address this, we adapt a scoring rule posterior based on a strictly proper scoring rule, following the generalized Bayes framework. We then propose a block SGMCMC within Gibbs sampling mechanism. This enables efficient exploration of high-dimensional parameter spaces by identifying a sparse representation of neural implicit generative models. We demonstrate the performance of our proposed method through experiments on $p \gg n$ linear regression and an application of neural generative models.

papers.title: Accelerated Concatenation of Stepsize Schedules for Smooth Strongly Convex Gradient Descent
papers.abstract: This work considers stepsize schedules for gradient descent on smooth strongly convex objectives. We develop a curvature-dependent concatenation framework for constructing stepsize schedules of arbitrary length with sharp worst-case guarantees. Within this framework, we introduce two families of schedules for the function-value gap and gradient norm of the last iterate, respectively. For each fixed condition number $κ=L/μ>1$, both families attain iteration complexity $Θ(κ^ρ\log(1/ε))$ for sufficiently small $ε$, where $ρ=\log_{\sqrt2+1}2\approx0.7864$. This complexity is optimal up to a subpolynomial factor in $κ$ among predetermined nonnegative stepsize schedules. The framework also recovers the strongly convex silver schedule at power-of-two iteration budgets and applies to smooth convex and smooth weakly convex functions.

papers.title: Logarithmic Regret for Alternating Mirror Descent
papers.abstract: Alternating online mirror descent (AltOMD) is a simple learning rule for zero-sum games, which improves upon simultaneous OMD numerically and theoretically. Previous work obtained $O(T^{1/3})$ and $O(T^{1/5})$ regret bounds for AltOMD, by leveraging modified-energy-function-based analyses. However, settling whether AltOMD achieves near-constant regret has remained an open question. In this paper we resolve the question of whether AltOMD achieves near-constant regret in the affirmative. In particular, we show an $O(log(T))$ regret bound on the sum of the players' external regrets for any two-player zero-sum bilinear game with compact convex strategy sets, under mild regularity assumptions on the regularizers. We verify that our assumptions hold for the negative entropy regularizer, thereby obtaining logarithmic regret for the alternating multiplicative weights updates algorithm. The regret bound also yields an $O(log(T)/T)$ duality gap bound for the averaged strategies.

papers.title: Reality and Perceptual Gaps in Expressive Swarm Robotics
papers.abstract: Moving robot swarms from simulation into the physical world can be difficult because small discrepancies in hardware, timing and communication can cascade across interacting robots and alter group behaviour. This challenge is known as the reality gap. When swarms operate in human environments, a second challenge emerges: a perceptual gap between what the swarm physically does and what human onlookers actually perceive. This study examines the same decentralised coordination code deployed across three robotic swarms-tabletop, aerial and human-scale mobile manipulators-during live artistic performances. We find that while the underlying algorithms executed reliably on all three platforms, physical embodiment drastically altered visible motion-distorting execution timescales by more than a factor of three and reshaping trajectory geometry. More importantly, audience surveys revealed that human interpretation does not mirror technical success: how observers attribute meaning (perceived purpose) and how they react emotionally (comfort versus threat) depend heavily on physical form. Meaning attribution and emotional responses did not vary together. Our results demonstrate that successfully transferring swarm software to physical hardware is insufficient for real-world deployment. Addressing the reality gap does not guarantee that the resulting collective motion will be readily interpreted by human observers. Swarms destined for human environments must be engineered not only for decentralised stability but also for the expressive physical dynamics through which humans interpret collective motion.

papers.title: A Fully Polynomial Approximation Algorithm for the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick Model
papers.abstract: Montanari's incremental approximate message passing (IAMP) algorithm [FOCS 2019; SIAM J. Comput., 2025] and the zero-temperature formulation of El Alaoui, Montanari and Sellke (AMS) [Ann. Probab., 2021] find a $(1-\varepsilon)$ approximation to the maximum Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) energy in $C(\varepsilon)N^2$ operations for fixed accuracy, with probability tending to one as $N\to\infty$, under their respective full-support and access-model assumptions. However, it was unknown whether this approximation could be achieved with work polynomial in both $N$ and $1/\varepsilon$, together with quantitative guarantees at finite dimension. Under the same assumptions as AMS, we introduce grouped IAMP with exact Gaussian query outputs (GEG-IAMP), which is the first SK approximation algorithm with total work polynomial in $N$ and $1/\varepsilon$ and a finite-size guarantee above a dimension threshold polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$ and $\log(1/α)$. More precisely, for every $α\in(0,1/2)$, it returns a $(1-\varepsilon)$ approximation with probability at least $1-α$ whenever $N\ge \mathsf{K}\varepsilon^{-2}\log^2(e/\varepsilon)\log(\mathsf{K}/α)$, using $O(N^2/\varepsilon)$ work and $O(N^2)$ storage. GEG-IAMP replaces the Onsager correction by Reeves's coupling construction [arXiv:2508.10782] and groups Euler-Maruyama steps into $O(1/\varepsilon)$ matrix-vector products. We also prove a relative guarantee for AMS IAMP with $O(N^2\varepsilon^{-3}\log^2(e/\varepsilon))$ work but a sufficient dimension exponential in inverse accuracy. By returning a fixed configuration below its dimension threshold, GEG-IAMP also provides an asymptotic fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme (AFPRAS), with an additive error independent of dimension.

papers.title: Anisotropic Minkowski flows: well-posedness and asymptotic behaviour
papers.abstract: We study anisotropic Minkowski-type curvature flows associated with a perimeter defined through oscillations on Wulff neighbourhoods. The anisotropy may be non-smooth, and in particular crystalline, while the mobility may differ from the anisotropy, provided a natural compatibility condition is satisfied. We compute the first variation of the perimeter and introduce a weak formulation in terms of distance functions and measure-valued nonlocal Cahn-Hoffman fields. By means of a nonlocal minimising movement scheme and suitable estimates for the evolution of Wulff shapes, we prove existence of weak superflows and subflows starting from arbitrary closed sets. Under the additional assumption that the initial level sets have compact boundary, a comparison principle yields existence and uniqueness of the level set flow. Finally, we prove that variational weak flows converge, up to fattening, as $r\searrow 0$ to the weak flow of the local anisotropic, possibly crystalline, curvature motion. The main step in the proof consists in averaging the nonlocal Cahn-Hoffman measures to obtain vector fields converging to a local Cahn-Hoffman field.

papers.title: Coherence and the Hilbert-syzygy identity for power series over valuation domains
papers.abstract: Let $V$ be a complete valuation domain of rank 1, and let $Γ$ be its value group. We investigate the power series ring $V[[t]]$, and finally answer the long standing question of when this ring is coherent. Specifically, we prove that it is coherent if and only if $V$ is almost maximal, and either $Γ= \mathbb{R}$ or $Γ$ is discrete. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the weak Hilbert-syzygy identity $w. dim V [[X]] = w. dim V + 1$ holds if and only if $V[[X]]$ is a coherent ring.

papers.title: The PAU Survey: Self-supervised image denoising for flux-preserving photometry
papers.abstract: Context. Deep photometric surveys increasingly rely on low signal-to-noise imaging, where noise affects source detection, flux measurements, photometric redshifts, and sample selection. Self-supervised denoising methods are attractive because they do not require ground-truth images, but applying them to quantitative photometry requires controlling the flux biases they may introduce. Aims. We evaluate and improve Noise2Void (N2V) for denoising real astronomical images, focusing on preserving fluxes, reducing photometric scatter, and retaining the main source features across a wide magnitude range. Methods. We use real observations from the Physics of the Accelerating Universe Survey (PAUS) together with PAUS-like simulated images. We show that standard N2V systematically underestimates galaxy fluxes, especially for faint galaxies. To mitigate this bias, we add a bounded-output layer that limits large negative outputs, and fine-tune the model with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and two flux-aware loss terms that preserve the flux scale and improve repeated-exposure flux consistency. Results. For PAUS galaxies with 22 <= i_AB < 23 in the NB645 band, the standard N2V flux-ratio distribution peaks far below unity, while the bounded-output model restores it close to the original PAUS flux scale. The flux-aware LoRA fine-tuning reduces the width of the repeated-exposure flux-difference distribution to sigma_68 = 0.529 in NB645, an effective 47% reduction in random flux scatter relative to the original PAUS uncertainty scale, while keeping the median flux ratio close to unity. Conclusions. Denoising methods for astronomical surveys must be evaluated with photometric diagnostics, not image-quality metrics alone. With flux-aware modifications, self-supervised denoising can be adapted to low-SNR survey images while preserving the flux information needed for quantitative analysis.

papers.title: Localisations of rings of weak global dimension at most one
papers.abstract: We characterise the commutative rings of weak global dimension at most one whose derived categories can be stratified by the Balmer-Favi support theory. For such rings, this yields a bijective correspondence between the class of localising subcategories of the derived category, and the subsets of the Zariski spectrum. For a large class of rings of weak global dimension at most one including all valuation domains, this occurs if and only if the ring is locally strongly discrete, if and only if the Telescope conjecture holds, and if and only if the module category has Gabriel dimension. However, we also give an example of a valuation domain where all these conditions fail, and yet the residue fields generate its derived category and we can classify all the localising subcategories of $D(R)$. Additionally, in the same example, we show that the Balchin-Stevenson smashing support cannot stratify $D(R)$ either.

papers.title: Geometric classification of imaginaries in pseudofinite fields
papers.abstract: In [Pil07], Pillay showed that every imaginary in a proper pair of algebraically closed fields is interalgebraic with an imaginary of a certain algebraic form. In this paper, we establish an analogue for lovely pairs of pseudofinite fields. After naming countably many constants, we prove that every imaginary in lovely pairs of pseudofinite fields is interalgebraic with an imaginary of the same algebraic form as [Pil07] in the corresponding pairs of finite extensions of pseudofinite fields.

papers.title: Should the Action Expert Train the VLM? Action-Token Supervision and Gradient Routing in Mixture-of-Transformer VLAs
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly pair a pre-trained vision-language model (VLM) with a flow-matching expert that conditions its action predictions on the VLM's key-value representations. Those representations must carry information useful for control, yet the VLM was never trained for the action expert's flow-matching objective. Two signals can address this: gradients backpropagated from the expert's loss (coupling), or VLM supervision to predict discrete tokens encoding the same target actions. Prominent training recipes forgo the first, blocking expert-to-VLM gradients (insulation) to protect the VLM's existing capabilities, while also supervising it on vision-language data and action tokens. Because vision-language co-training also aims to preserve those capabilities, the additional protection provided by insulation is unclear. At the same time, insulation removes a direct signal about which features continuous action prediction requires. On the other hand, action-token supervision offers an alternative way to learn action-relevant representations, which may explain why insulation succeeds in practice. We disentangle these factors in autonomous driving and manipulation by independently varying action-token supervision and whether the expert's loss updates the VLM. In open-loop driving, insulation is competitive with coupling when action tokens are supervised; without them, coupling reduces trajectory-prediction error by roughly 25%. When both components are trained jointly from the outset, coupling increases closed-loop driving route progress by approximately 17% with action-token supervision and 40% without it, and similarly improves robot manipulation performance under both settings. These findings show that the value of gradient insulation depends on the VLM's action supervision and the evaluation setting, challenging insulation as a default VLA training recipe.

papers.title: The sum-of-squares complexity of linear-algebraic principles
papers.abstract: We study the degree needed for sum-of-squares (SoS) proofs of several basic principles of real linear algebra. For any $n\times n$ matrix $A$ of rank greater than $r$, the Weak Rank Principle states that the equations $XY^\top=A$ with $n\times r$ matrix variables $X, Y$ have no solution. We show that this principle requires degree exactly $2r+2$ to prove. On the other hand, for $A=I_n$, setting $X = Y$ gives the Tight Frame Principle, which has a degree-$4$ proof. For $n\times n$ matrices, proving that a right inverse is also a left inverse requires degree exactly $2n+2$, while proving that orthonormal rows imply orthonormal columns again has a degree-4 proof. Using our lower bounds, we also derive related SoS degree lower bounds for polynomial systems encoding sign rank, matrix rigidity, small-width homogeneous non-commutative algebraic branching programs, and tensor CP rank.
